records.title: Translating climate-smart agriculture into practice: the role of national research systems and the Brazilian ABC Plan
records.authors: Maria Victoria Folkerts Cincurá; Luis Eduardo Pacifici Rangel; Bruno dos Santos Alves Figueiredo Brasil
records.abstract: During the 20th century, the proliferation of agricultural innovations and research led to significant increases in yield, improvements in food security and human health, poverty reduction, and a raise in economic outputs (Rosegrant et al., 2023;Nin-Pratt & Stads, 2023). Rosegrant et al. (2023) propose that agricultural research is "one of the interventions with the highest return in all of agriculture and global development" (p. 182). They argue that investment in agricultural research is a costbeneficial strategy to reduce poverty and hunger as well as address climate change.Aimed at aiding public policy-making, agricultural research is mainly conducted by two types of stakeholders (Rosegrant et al., 2023). On the one hand, international research organizations, like the Consortium of International Agricultural Research Centers (CGIAR), have a crucial role in conducting research that shapes global policy-making agendas and in sharing scientific knowledge between countries. On the other hand, national agricultural research systems' mostly conduct nationally relevant research and have an important role to adapt innovations to local contexts.Global agricultural spending grew by 50% between 2000-2016(Nin-Pratt & Stads, 2023). In particular, funding for research on the Global South's agrifood sector was around $60 billion US dollars per year during the period of 2010-2019 (Prasad et al., 2023). From that total, less than 7% focuses explicitly on delivering environmental outcomes, and less than 5% on social outcomes. About two-thirds of this funding originates from national governments, which allocated 10-13% of their yearly agricultural budgets to research. This expansion was driven largely by middle-income countries after the 2008 global food price spike (Rosegrant et al., 2023), while investment stagnated in high-income countries and declined in low-income countries (Nin-Pratt & Stads, 2023). China, India and Brazil alone accounted for nearly 40% of total innovation funding (Prasad et al., 2023). Private corporations and equity investors contribute 15-25% and 2-3% of the total funding, respectively (Prasad et al., 2023), with global private spending on agricultural research tripling between 1990 and 2014 (Nin-Pratt & Stads, 2023). Development partners, including philanthropic and multilateral agencies, provide around 8% of total funding but have increasingly shifted support from innovation generation toward scaling and local adaptation, which is an area where national agricultural research systems remain indispensable (Prasad et al., 2023).In this paper, we discuss the macro-level dynamics between international research organizations and national research systems. It argues for the importance of national research systems to adapt and support implementation of international concepts in local contexts. The rise of the climatesmart agriculture (CSA) concept in the global research agenda led by international organizations and the implementation of the ABC Plan in Brazil supported by Embrapa, the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation, will be set as a case study to demonstrate such dynamics. Finally, it concludes with a call for investments in national agricultural research systems.2 The rise of CSA to the global policy-making agenda As one of the several frameworks that emerged to push for more sustainable and productive agriculture, climate-smart agriculture (CSA) was first formally launched by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) at the Hague Conference of Food Security, Agriculture and Climate Change (FAO, 2010). The term was then defined as "an approach to developing the technical, policy and investment conditions to achieve sustainable agricultural development for food security under climate change" (FAO, 2013, p. 9). CSA's goal can be defined as threefold: (i) sustainably increase agricultural productivity and food security, (ii) adapt and build resilience to climate change, and (iii) reduce/remove atmospheric greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions where possible (Lipper et al., 2014). Also referred to as the "triple win" of productivity, adaptation, and mitigation. Unlike prescriptive approaches based on technological packages, CSA was conceived as a guiding framework capable of integrating agricultural, environmental, climate, and rural development policies. The literature highlights that this formulation was an explicit response to the limitations of conventional intensification policies, which sought productivity gains without measuring climate risks or impacts on ecosystems (Lipper et al., 2014;Thornton et al., 2018).At a time where the international community was increasingly acknowledging the interactions between climate change and agriculture, such as during the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Conference of Parties (COP)15 and COP16, the concept was quickly adopted and promoted by a variety of global-level stakeholders (Newell, 2017). Research to assess which agricultural practices deliver on the "triple win" quickly popularized, providing evidence on trade-offs between practices and rapidly increasing awareness of context sensitivity for implementation (Smith et al., 2020). International research organizations and international non-governmental organizations (INGOs) contributed to evidence of generation and capacity-building. For example, FAO's Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook (2013) provided guidance for countries on CSA policymaking and implementation. The CGIAR, particularly the Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS) program, promoted the idea through country profiles, toolkits, and research-policy engagement.Multilateral institutions then translated this evidence into policy recommendations, aligning it with financing mechanisms, and establishing measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) systems (Freed et al., 2023). Multilateral development banks, such as the World Bank, mainstreamed CSA through lending instruments and climate finance mechanisms. Bilateral donors, including the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the European Union (EU), funded pilot programs and capacity-building initiatives that further embedded CSA into national policy frameworks.The concept came to influence national public policies and international agreements. Elements of CSA increasingly appeared in National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) and multilateral funding programs (Campbell et al., 2016). Global South countries, such as Brazil, India, Kenya, and Ethiopia, incorporated its principles into national sustainable agriculture programs. The result is that CSA ceased to be a technical FAO agenda and became a reference for low-carbon and climate-resilient agricultural policy-making.Despite its broad adoption, CSA has also been subject to critical scrutiny. The flexibility that makes CSA attractive as a policy framework has been criticized for allowing heterogeneous interpretations, uneven ambition levels, and, in some cases, limited accountability regarding mitigation outcomes (Newell, 2017;Totin et al., 2018). These critiques highlight that CSA is not a prescriptive solution, but rather a governance framework whose effectiveness depends on institutional design, monitoring capacity, and alignment with farmers' economic incentives.3 The Brazilian ABC Plan: The scientific-institutional translation of CSA into national policyThe ABC Plan (Plano Setorial de Mitigação e de Adaptação às Mudanças Climáticas para a Consolidação de uma Economia de Baixa Emissão de Carbono na Agricultura, or "Low-Carbon Agriculture Plan") is an example of how Global South countries can translate and implement international climate narratives into public policies rooted in local contexts. Although formulated before the consolidation of the CSA concept, the ABC Plan already reflected the central pillars of the climate-smart agriculture framework: sustainable productivity increases, enhanced adaptation and resilience, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions (Lipper et al., 2014). What makes the Brazilian experience particularly relevant is the centrality of tropical scientific knowledge accumulated over decades, combined with sustained public investment, institutional coordination, and credit-based policy instruments. Without these conditions, similar outcomes would be unlikely to emerge in other contexts. As demonstrated in various economic analyses, the Plan not only responded to international agendas but anticipated them by transforming scientific evidence into financing, credit, and governance instruments (Paixão & Bacha, 2015;Silva & Vieira Filho, 2020).Between 2010 and 2020, the ABC Plan enabled the adoption of sustainable agricultural technologies on 54.02 million hectares, mitigating the equivalent of 193.67 million tons of CO₂eq (MAPA, 2023). In integrated crop-livestock-forestry systems alone, there was an expansion of 10.76 million hectares, while an additional 26.8 million hectares of degraded pastures were recovered (Table 1). Furthermore, such practices contribute to the overall increase in livestock productivity, leading to a reduction in emission intensity per unit of product, while simultaneously slowing the expansion of pasturelands, which curbs CO₂ emissions associated with deforestation and preserves biodiversity (Paarlberg, 2025). The policy is currently in its second phase, called ABC+ Plan, which covers the period from 2021 to 2030 and sets a goal of expanding sustainable practices to an additional 72.68 million hectares, potentially resulting in mitigation of over 1 Gt of CO₂eq (MAPA, 2021).The design of the ABC Plan differs significantly from approaches focused exclusively on mitigation, typical of high-income countries. The Plan was deliberately structured around the productive priorities of Brazilian farmers: productivity gains, reduction of operational costs, stability in the face of climate variability, and restoration of soil fertility (MAPA, 2021). Climate benefits, such as carbon sequestration, methane reduction, and improved water infiltration, were conceived as cobenefits, not as the main driver for adoption. This logic aligns with the scientific literature on CSA in low-and middle-income countries, which demonstrates that climate policies only become scalable when linked to direct and measurable economic returns (Totin et al., 2018;Harvey et al., 2014). By placing income and resilience at the center, the ABC Plan avoided the common mistake of "carbonfirst" policies, often unable to gain traction among producers.The ABC Plan adopts a governance strategy based on State Management Committees (CGE/SSCs) that enables its scaled implementation. These committees bring together federal and state governments, research and technical assistance institutions, as well as organized civil society (MAPA, 2023). Their role is to mobilize producers through technology transfer that promote the adoption of the ABC's sustainable practices (Bragança et al., 2022;Vinholis et al., 2021). The CGEs also allow for adapting implementation to local operational conditions, resource availability, and long-term development dynamics in each Brazilian state (MAPA, 2023;Vinholis et al., 2021).Despite the advances, the Brazilian experience also highlights structural limitations in implementing climate-smart policies in the Global South. Persistent challenges include barriers to credit access, regional disparities in technical capacity, concentration of resources in the Center-South, and institutional weaknesses that limit uptake in the North and Northeast parts of the country (Lovato et al., 2020;Gianetti, 2021). These findings underscore the need for climate-smart policies to have national-level coherence combined with tailored implementation strategies for different regional contexts, robust monitoring systems, qualified technical assistance, and alignment between banks, research, and territorial governance. Technology alone is not sufficient: institutions, coordination, and state capacity matter as much as the suggested technical package (Conceição, 2022). This article does not aim to provide a causal impact evaluation of the ABC Plan. Instead, it offers an institutional and policy analysis of how national research systems contribute to translating global climate frameworks into scalable public policies. Importantly, the Brazilian experience should not be interpreted as a readily transferable model. Its outcomes reflect specific historical, institutional, and scientific trajectories, reinforcing the argument that CSA implementation pathways must be nationally grounded rather than globally standardized.International development organizations were crucial in shaping the policy-making agenda, financing mechanisms, and monitoring frameworks of CSA. International frameworks such as CSA and regenerative agriculture tend to circulate globally in an asymmetric manner, reflecting the scientific, economic, and normative interests of the Global North (Sabourin et al., 2021). The ABC Plan operates as a counterpoint to this dynamic. Far from being a mere recipient of external models, Brazil hybridized the principles of CSA with its tropical scientific base, its productive realities, and its development objectives. In doing so, it not only translated global concepts into applicable policies but contributed to reconfiguring them.Brazil's experience shows that national agricultural research systems have an important role in generating innovations, monitoring implementation, and scaling for maximizing impact across the CSA pillars. There needs to be greater recognition of the role of national systems in advancing the food systems transition and their capacity to generate context-specific innovations and scale climate-smart solutions across different regions. The Brazilian trajectory also demonstrates that successful climatesmart transitions in the Global South emerge from the combination of local science, institutional innovation, and policies designed based on farmers' priorities.We therefore call for a Global South-led agricultural research agenda, supported by increased investment from national governments and international development funders, to ensure that global standards and priorities reflect the ecological and socio-productive realities of the region's most central to the future of global food systems. However, investments in agricultural research systems alone will not efficiently transform food systems (Nin-Pratt & Stads, 2023). System-level funding and knowledge exchange between countries are essential to unlock human capacity and research systems, enabling their success in producing, implementing, and scaling innovation.

records.title: Is Japan's Economic Strength Rooted in its Business Discourse Model?
records.abstract: It is often said that Japan's cultural practices stand out as particularly interesting and/or unique.As Hofstede says, "Societies are historically, organically developed forms of social organization.Strictly speaking, the concept of a common culture applies to societies, not to nations."Despite the diverse origins and plural nature of Japanese society, Japan is often perceived as a monoethnic group with one language and one common culture.Whatever the complex nature through which Japanese culture has evolved, the Japanese people, numbering 127 million, have been living in a land area equivalent to 0.3% of the global landmass on an archipelago where approximately 67% of the country is mountainous, leaving little space for industries and dwellings.This crowding has fostered a rich sense of sharing and community.This mini state is the third largest national economy in the world in terms of GDP, the world's second largest developed economy, and the world's largest creditor with a surplus of over $3 trillion.How could this tiny state with a limited land area become such a strong economy?This paper will inquire into the secrets of Japan's economic strength from a business communication perspective, arguing that it is the cultural and communicative practices of the Japanese people that have helped it achieve its success.The paper will present the hypothesis that Japanese economic strength is based on a unique business discourse, itself rooted in particular cultural practices.This business discourse is focused on the widespread sharing of information within enterprises, leading to reductions in uncertainty, improved ability to assess risks, successful strategies regarding process technologies and market development, and big productivity improvements.Japan is No.27 out of 59 countries in the IMD's 2012 World Competitiveness Rankings (Top 3 are HK, US, and Switzerland) after Taiwan (7th), Malaysia (14th), and Korea (22nd).According to IMD, China is No.1 and Japan is No.10 in terms of international investment.Japan is No.40 out of 59 countries in the management education ranking (Top countries are Switzerland, Singapore, Belgium, Iceland, Finland, etc.)The purpose of this paper is to rebut his one-sided and negative comments on Japan's economic strength and to show that Japan is still a strong economic nation and that this strength comes in large part from the Japanese business discourse model.A strong economic nation possesses long-lived business enterprises.Unlike the case in many other economies, Japanese companies often have very long lives.According to one report, the average life expectancy of an MNC listed in the Fortune 500 is between 40 and 50 years.Japanese companies seem to go entirely against this trend.Abegglen (2006), who first introduced the Japanese Management System to the world, has noted as follows :The oldest kaisha [company], and probably the oldest company in the world, is Kongo-gumi, founded in 578 and run by the 40th generation of the Kongo family.It is based in Osaka and specializes in temple construction and general contracting.The second oldest is probably Hoshi, a hotel management firm founded in 718, run by the 46th generation.Among listed companies, the oldest is Surugaya founded in 1461, before Columbus set off for America, and still a favored producer of Japanese sweets (p.13).Many other listed companies also have histories of several hundred years.Many of these long-lived companies, rich in history and wisdom, are still very active with excellent performance, fostering high sales turnover and profits in global business.More than three hundred Japanese long-lived companies are ranked among the world's top producers.Moreover, among the top twenty of these companies several have global market shares of 100% (they have no global competition).Japan's economic success, as exemplified by its long-lived companies, is owed to the genius of building a management system based closely on cultural practices developed over Japan's long history.Taking this view, the paper will discuss Japan's overall business discourse styles, highlighting some features such as Ho-Ren-So.This is an acronym employing the first syllables of Hokoku (Reporting), Renraku (Contacting) and Sodan (Consulting).It is a continual and collaborative communication process between superiors, subordinates, and colleagues over the course of a project.Ho-Ren-So is a typical business communication practice particular to Japanese culture, in which great importance is placed upon cooperation 同志社商学 第６ ５巻 第４号(２ ０ １ ４年１月) ２( 304) within a group.It is one example from among several that illustrate how Japanese cultural practices provide a dynamic force that helps lead businesses to success.In sum, Japan is not an economically waning country as IMD and its dean have claimed.Japan is still a really strong country. (JFTC, 2012) notes that Japan is the fourth largest international trading nation in terms of gross exports and imports.Its annual publication, Foreign Trade 2012 (JFTC, Vol.37, p.112, 2012), notes that Japan has huge foreign reserves, amounting to $1.06 trillion.Iwamoto (2012, pp.41-52), a Tokyo-based financial consultant, claims that the level of the Japanese people's net savings is the largest in the world at about $15 trillion.Her claim is supported by James Takahashi (2013), who states in a column entitled "The largest amount of savings in the world with zero interest" : Japanese people have the highest amount of savings compared to any other country approximately $15 trillion US dollars (3 times Japan's GDP, almost equivalent to the US GDP).However, Japan has experienced historically low interest rates on savings, near zero percent.Thus many Japanese tend to move extra money overseas to take advantage of safe international investments with higher Is Japan's Economic Strength Rooted in its Business Discourse Model?(Kameda)yields.Sugashita (2013), an economist and consultant for international finance, notes in his latest book, Buy Japan, the World's Most Powerful Nation, that more than 95% of the creditors of Japan's national debt, who mostly are the holders of the national bonds, are Japanese people and businesses.This is quite different from the cases of the US, Greece, Spain, Portugal, etc.Moreover, Japan has not issued even a single national bond in a foreign currency, only in Japanese yen (p.148-152).p.22) says there are no companies lasting over one hundred years in Korea.He cites an article in The Chosun Ilbo, one of the leading Korean newspapers, reporting that in Korea there are only a few companies whose history exceeds eighty years, such as Kyunsung Bongiae, Samyang Holdings Corporation, Yuhan Corporation, etc. Nomura (2007) claims that in China there are several long-lived companies, mainly those producing herbal medicine, such as Beijing Tong Ren Tang (founded in 1669), the world's largest herbal pharmacist.Recordchina (2012), a Chinese online information provider, however, reports that in China there are only five companies that have a history of more than 150 years, such as the already noted Tong Ren Tang, Liubiju, a pickle shop founded in 1538, Zhang Xiao Quan, a scissor manufacturer founded in 1663, Chenliji, another herbal druggist, and Wanglaoji, a beverage 2 producer.Izumiya (2007) listed twenty long-lived companies in his book and analyzed the reasons why they have survived for so long.He noted that these companies all share the same conditions : they have been in business more than one hundred years ; they compete in world markets with cutting-edge technology ; and they maintain dominant market shares with their products (p.2).Long-lived Japanese companies share these characteristics.Japanese management success probably is rooted in the traditional structure of Japanese dwellings.It is often records.title: Climbing a Macro–Micro Consistency Learning Curve: Emerging Market Challenges for the Next Decade
records.abstract: This edition of the Journal of Development Perspectives focuses on key economic policy challenges facing emerging economies now and in the foreseeable few years. Our authors were asked to reflect on how countries have addressed existing constraints to economic growth in recent years, pulling together lessons and providing perspective on how both these and newer challenges can be better tackled in future. Authors chose to look at these questions from a range of economic and political economy perspectives, covering an array of emerging and developing countries in West Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, alongside South Africa, Brazil, and Indonesia. The articles highlight challenges to economic growth from macroeconomic policy, climate change, the emergence of Covid-19, and permanent and seemingly ubiquitous political obstacles to change.Three broad themes emerge from our authors’ contributions.One is that appropriate open-macroeconomic policy frameworks remain a key challenge, especially for countries in the process of becoming emerging market economies. A second is that bedding down appropriate macroeconomic frameworks in emerging economies continues to be at risk from local responses to domestic challenges and to global events. Often, these responses are guided by newer or, more commonly, rebooted narratives that undermine the somewhat older, post-Asian crisis approach to macro policy that was evident in emerging economies in the 2000s. A third is that part of the challenge to the second theme is whether or not countries need better alignment between macroeconomic objectives and microeconomic dynamics. This harks back to another literature – on time consistency, real business cycles and the new Keynesian synthesis – many emerging economies appear to be caught in a tension between macroeconomics and microeconomics. The danger is that these tensions lead to big macroeconomic policy mistakes.In the remainder of this chapter, I review the contributions of our authors and provide some perspective on the themes raised by them.For many countries, as in both West and southern Africa, exchange rate regimes remain in flux. Choices to further anchor fixed regimes or to go for greater autonomy with inflation targets and floating rates remain critically important questions. These topics are explored in the contributions by Nonso Obikili and by Andreas Wörgötter and Zuzana Brixiova.Nonso Obikili takes on the role of exchange rate policies within broader frameworks including inflation targets and central bank independence in West Africa. Obikili looks, in particular, at how Ghana, Guinea, and Nigeria have worked to maintain best practice macro policies generally, while allowing exchange rate policies to deviate from them, becoming obstacles to stronger growth.The problem comes from two sources. One is an historical economic legacy, in which mono-export economies remain hindered by outdated economic policies and arrangements that work against diversification. The other is related—a failure to reconstruct the aims of fiscal and monetary policy, because important interest groups can be negatively affected by it. The challenge is created by historical pegs to advanced economy currencies, not least the French franc, which create an expectation of cheap imports for elites and induced the growth of firms reliant on imported capital goods. The implied political constraint and the other economic constraint, together have severely limited policy autonomy. But they have also become constraints to diversification and integration, making it difficult for these countries to diversify out of being mono-export economies.In recent times, these dynamics have been made more rigid by a further failure to use extraordinary export proceeds to shift policy in meaningful ways. As Obikili sets out, the challenge is well established: Where economies are dependent on commodity exports or a narrow range of exports, the temptation is high for countries to use boom periods to diversify sources of economic growth. But this often fails, and both governments and middle classes realign their expectations around exchange rate stability rather than more inclusive growth. Over time, this preference extends to the monetary authority, which, despite being independent, comes to define its mandate as currency stability, and often overvalued.The result, combined with the reality of cyclical commodity prices, has been long periods of overvaluation that developed further politically inspired underpinnings, in particular legislative limits on flexibility. These constraints thus took on, over time, institutional characteristics, making them even harder to change, and increasing the incidence of exchange rate-induced macroeconomic instability. Although Obikili is circumspect about the utility of floating rates, because of underdeveloped currencies and financial and capital markets in these countries, he makes a sensible case for the establishment of objective measures of exchange rate levels and embedding them into monetary policy frameworks.Andreas Wörgötter and Zuzana Brixiova also draw our attention to the importance of credible currency regimes and their macroeconomic underpinnings for stability in financial systems and successful, long-term economic convergence of developing and emerging economies. For regions like Sub-Saharan Africa, taking steps toward fixed exchange rate frameworks, perhaps as a waypoint on the path to monetary union, could provide credibility that individual countries struggle to attain on their own. Bringing in more fixed arrangements, can, in their view, act as agents of restraint on unsustainable policies for many small economies and enable greater stability achieved at lower costs. Anchoring that policy effort in a path toward monetary union could further strengthen credibility. The authors point to a surprisingly large set of successful empirical examples.Although it is well understood that monetary unions and fixed exchange rate regimes among countries with heterogeneous economies are difficult to sustain, the authors note that heterogeneity can be accommodated in regimes with one dominant member and diverse countries willing to ensure flexible internal pricing systems and/or other macroeconomic policies that are sufficiently flexible to accommodate the pegs. This opens up the question of what might work for African economies, which are heterogeneous and do not match up well to OCA criteria. The authors focus on the Common Monetary Area (CMA) centered on South Africa and including Namibia, Lesotho, and Eswatini.The conclusion of this analysis is that very open small economies can benefit from being in fixed exchange rate arrangements with dominant currency economies so long as they can also implement other forms of flexibility. These can be in major markets that determine relative price differentials, like labor markets, or where they can run highly countercyclical fiscal policy. The key issue is how the economy responds to shocks when there is complete loss of monetary policy independence and no currency flexibility. The trade-off is not complete here, however, as the gains from “borrowing” monetary credibility and financial stability can be thought of as complementing flexible macrostructural policies. If structural flexibility allows CMA members to benefit more than they would otherwise from integration, then the trade-off is optimized for those countries. Wörgötter and Brixiova use a convergence equation with South African provinces and the small CMA member countries plus Botswana to assess this optimization process, revealing that Namibia is performing well within the CMA, whereas Botswana achieves a superior growth performance outside the CMA.A second central theme is the bedding down and implementation of sustainable inflation targeting and floating rate macroeconomic frameworks in the context of increasingly open global financial and capital markets.If in the 1980s advanced economies moved macroeconomic and microeconomic policies in closer alignment, and learned to live with increasing financial integration, those adaptations arguably only truly confronted emerging economies in the same way late in the 1990s and into the 2000s. The Asian crisis and its prolonged aftermath underscored the weaknesses in macroeconomic frameworks that promised quasi-fixed exchange rates but also facilitated large current account deficits. One response to this was a shift to more use of inflation-targeting frameworks and floating rates, backed up with reserve accumulation when possible.As that move to flexible currencies picked up steam, however, the global financial crisis (GFC) reminded us that the increasingly interconnected global economy depended in many ways on hegemonic and structurally supercompetitive positions—in finance in the US dollar and in trade between China, East Asia, and the advanced economies of the West.1 Part of the developmental critique of macroeconomic policies in the 2000s arose from emerging economies’ experience with appreciating real exchange rates after the crisis. This analysis took different forms, but centered on the idea that emerging markets that had liberalized financial accounts suffered from capital inflows.2Over time, this critique shifted focus to a stronger dollar.3 As the US economy recovered and raised interest rates, the dollar strengthened and increased the cost of credit to these economies and, wherever trade was invoiced in the dollar, also made them uncompetitive. This suggested that the monetary autonomy created by inflation targeting plus floating exchange rates was less effective than previously believed and led some to search for solutions promising more autonomy. Less noticed was that USD strength tended to dampen inflation in many emerging economies, creating the false impression that continued fiscal expansion and low interest rates were sustainable settings. When economic growth slowed, in part due to evolutions in trade and China’s deceleration, discussed later, these illusions were exposed, and macroeconomic policy was forced to adjust, contributing to severe economic downturns in countries like Brazil.With the Trump Administration and advent of unconventional approaches to world trade, many of the certainties around global supply chains and policy moderation that underpinned the great moderation of the 2000s came progressively undone. Trade disputes threatened to upend supply chains first. Second, the Covid-19 pandemic came along to radically reduce certainty about both international and domestic economic arrangements and their logistical, physical, and financial sustainability.These shocks raise various policy concerns for emerging economies. One is about how they fit into global supply chains—how single-minded should efforts be to slot in? And a second is about how to further generate more independent macroeconomic policy space, both relative to the US dollar and to the rest of the world but also, critically, domestically.4 Part of the rethink of policy that all this engendered was the idea that the GFC was a massive demand shock, leading to low inflation, and that the key response to this had to be government spending and quantitative easing to prevent deflation from tipping into depression. While neat for advanced economies, it was less clear how useful this was for emerging markets, where, at the break of the GFC, most were in good macroeconomic shape. This makes it all the more remarkable that so many large emerging economies shifted policy quite far in the 2010s. records.title: Hayek: A Life, 1899–1950, by BruceCaldwell and HansjörgKlausinger (University of Chicago Press, Chicago, 2022), pp. 840.
records.abstract: In a review of a recent biography of Milton Friedman, Robert Skidelsky ranked John Maynard Keynes, Friedman and Friedrich Hayek at the ‘apex’ of the economics profession in the twentieth century (Skidelsky, 2024, p. 24). The contributions of Keynes and Friedman are better known perhaps than those of Hayek, at least in the Anglosphere. But Hayek: A Life, 1899–1950 (HAL1), the first of a projected two-volume biography, will almost certainly enhance the awareness and understanding of Hayek's life and writing. The authors are distinguished historians of economic thought: Bruce Caldwell is a research professor of economics and director of the Center for the History of Political Economy at Duke, while Hansjörg Klausinger is associate professor emeritus in the Department of Economics at WU Vienna University of Economics and Business. They are highly respected internationally for their published work on Hayek, Caldwell in particular as the general editor of the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek. HAL1 covers the first 50 years of Hayek's life, from his birth in Vienna in 1899 until he left London for Chicago in 1950; the second volume will focus on the final four decades of his life, concluding with his death in Freiburg, Germany, in 1992. About Hayek, the authors begin by stating the obvious fact that ‘His was a twentieth century life’ (HAL1, p. 10). Hayek's family, on both sides, were middle-ranking members of the Austrian nobility; several of the males were university professors. Hayek's father was a medical doctor and botanist; he was often invited to lecture at the university on aspects of his botanical work. Friedrich – or Fritz, as he was better known – was the eldest of three brothers; all three were to occupy professorial positions at universities in Austria, Germany, England and the United States. At age 17, Fritz was drafted into the Austrian army, serving on the Italian front in the final years of the First World War. With the ending of the war, which resulted in defeat for Austria and the dismemberment of the Hapsburg Empire, Hayek enrolled at the University of Vienna, studying a variety subjects, including economics, politics, law, philosophy and psychology. He completed two degrees, one in law, the other in politics. The authors assert that at the university ‘he learned from his new friends among the Jewish intelligentsia just how circumscribed his [school] education had been’ (HAL1, p. 12). But with the guidance of Friedrich von Weiser, one of his professors at the University of Vienna, and with the mentoring he received from another member of the Austrian School of Economics, Ludwig von Mises, who was to continue to play a key role in his subsequent career, Hayek quickly made up for a somewhat lacklustre academic performance at school. …a knack for being in the right place at the right time. He knew … all of the principals of the Austrian School of Economics; his grandfather was a climbing friend of Eugen Bohm-Bawerk, Friedrich von Weiser was his teacher, Ludwig von Mises was his mentor, and Joseph Schumpeter wrote letters of introduction for him to economists he knew in America. He came to America just as its leading economist, the institutionalist Wesley Clair Mitchell, was about to become the President of the American Economic Association. He sat in on his classes and took back with him enough knowledge to become the head of a business cycle institute. He arrived in England just at the right time to challenge Keynes, but also to participate in Lionel Robbins's Grand Seminar at the London School of Economics, where the formalism of most of what we think now of intermediate microeconomic theory was developed. He went to the University of Chicago just as the Chicago School of Economics was taking shape. (HAL1, pp. 12–13) Hayek, however, faced acute criticism from Keynes and his associates at Cambridge, who were recommending greater expenditure on public works and lower interest rates to offset rising unemployment. Replying to Hayek's critical review of his book, A Treatise on Money, Keynes declared that Hayek had ‘not read my book with that measure of “good will” which an author is entitled to expect of a reader. Until he can do so, he will not see what I mean or whether I am right’ (Skidelsky, 1992, pp. 456–7). About Hayek's Prices and Production, Keynes judged it to be ‘one of the most frightful muddles I have ever read … It is an extraordinary example of how, starting with a mistake, a remorseless logician can end in Bedlam’ (Skidelsky, 1992, pp. 296–7). Although there was never a meeting of minds, when Hayek learnt of Keynes's death in1946 he wrote that Keynes ‘was the one really great man I ever knew, and for whom I had unbounded admiration. The world will be a very much poorer place without him’ (Skidelsky, 2000, p. 472). Earlier, when the LSE moved to Cambridge during the war when the bombing of London by the Luftwaffe was at its peak, Keynes reached out to assist Hayek and his family, for which they were exceedingly grateful. Whether Keynes and Hayek sat together on the roof of King's College night after night watching for German aircraft on bombing missions is doubtful, but Keynes certainly arranged high table dining rights for Hayek at King's and nominated him for membership of the British Academy. With the publication of Keynes' General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936, and the favourable response it received in due course, Hayek refocused his attention, concentrating thereafter on the shortcomings of collectivism and central planning. In contrast to the new orthodoxy of government intervention in economic affairs, Hayek highlighted the benefits of the price mechanism as a more efficient economic system. The market process, he stressed, was a simple, yet highly effective device for preserving equilibrium between supply and demand, whereas collectivism and planning inevitably led to imbalances, over-production, unemployment and eventual enslavement. These themes constituted the essence Hayek's most famous and best-selling book, The Road to Serfdom, published in 1944. When Keynes read the book on his way to the United States for the World Monetary Conference at Bretton Woods he wrote to Hayek praising the work, declaring that it was ‘a grand book’, and claiming that ‘we all have the greatest reason to be grateful to you for saying so well what needs so much to be said … Morally and philosophically I find myself in agreement with virtually the whole of it, and not only in agreement, but in a deeply moved agreement’ (Skidelsky, 2000, p. 284). …where to draw the line. You agree that the line has to be drawn somewhere, and that the logical extreme is not possible. But you give us no guidance whatever as to where to draw it. It is true that you and I would probably draw it in different places. I should guess that according to my ideas you greatly under-estimate the practicability of the middle course. But as soon as you admit that the extreme is not possible … you are, on your own argument, done for, since you are trying to persuade us that so soon as one moves an inch in the planned direction you are necessarily launched on the slippery path which will lead you in due course over the precipice. (Skidelsky, 2000, p. 285) Caldwell and Klausinger explain that Hayek did not devote all of his time to writing and teaching. In the years immediately preceding the Second World War he thought about the possibility of establishing an international conference or organisation devoted to highlighting the benefits of liberalism and the shortcomings of socialism. In 1947 he arranged for a group of like-minded scholars, writers and journalists to meet for 2 weeks at Mont Pelerin in Switzerland to discuss the advantages of a liberal society and how it could be advanced. As the authors explain at some length, the idea owed much to Hayek's conversations with the American political journalist, Walter Lippmann, and the creation of the Colloque Lippmann, which met in Paris in August 1937 to discuss the deficiencies of collectivism and the virtues of liberalism. The Mont Pelerin Society continues to meet at different locations around the world; it is meeting this year in New Delhi. The Society played a significant part in the revival of neoliberalism between the 1960s and the 1990s. The final chapters of the book focus on the nature and consequences of the breakdown in 1950 of Hayek's first marriage to Hella von Frisch. Hayek was clearly the responsible party, deserting as he did a seemingly loving wife and his two children. The break-up also led to him losing his best friend, Lionel Robbins, who clearly supported Hella. The marriage breakdown was the principal reason why Hayek chose to leave London permanently. For Hayek it was a dramatic development, without doubt the most traumatic of his life. In 1938 he had become a British citizen; while he never returned to the UK to live after he left in1950, he retained his British citizenship throughout his life. Since this is the first volume of a two-volume biography, the authors make no attempt to sum-up Hayek's achievements, leaving that presumably for the second volume. One of the many impressive aspects of this first volume is the stated intention of the authors at the outset not to write a hagiography. In this they largely succeed. Another significant aspect of the book is the immense research the authors have undertaken, including considerable archival research and extensive interviews. Whatever one's view of Hayek, this is a major work in the history of economic thought and the authors deserve great praise for their achievement. It is strongly recommended.

records.title: Health-Seeking Behaviours of Indigenous Peoples in Bangladesh: A Narrative Review of Cultural Practices, Structural Barriers, and Pathways to Equity
records.abstract: Over 50 different ethnic groups make up Bangladesh’s Indigenous population, which suffers from severe health disparities stemming from social exclusion and historical marginalization. Designing successful and equitable health treatments requires an understanding of the intricate interactions between institutional barriers and cultural traditions, which are reflected in their health-seeking behaviors. This narrative review synthesizes two decades of evidence to map these behaviors and identify the trajectories for achieving health equity for these communities.We undertook a structured narrative review of the literature produced between the years 2000 and 2024. Databases such as PubMed, Google Scholar, and BanglaJOL were searched using the appropriate terms. The inclusion criteria included peer-reviewed publications and grey publications addressing the health practices of Indigenous people living in Bangladesh. The sources amounted to a total of 65, which were chosen for qualitative synthesis, and the results were structured into key theme-based areas.Our review confirms the reality of health-seeking as involving widespread medical pluralism, such that the traditional healer (e.g., kaviraj, shamans) remains the first line of care. Important access barriers for formal health care are multi-dimensional: (1) structural barriers like geographical isolation and economic barriers; (2) cultural and gender regimes which restrict the autonomy of women and a preference for culturally suitable care; and (3) limited health literacy which operates to restrict the use of preventive services. The factors result in drastic inequalities, particularly in maternal and mental health, which remain seriously undertreated. NGOs provide irreplaceable complementary services, but their advantage lies in decentralizing the benefit. The overriding finding is that even when the facilities operate, a lack of cultural safety and mistrust operate to restrict the use of the facilities.There is no one-size-fits-all approach that can be used to achieve health equity for Bangladesh’s Indigenous peoples. Interventions must be co-designed with communities, incorporating culturally safe methods, hiring health practitioners who speak Indigenous languages, and utilizing traditional healers’ trust. Enabling focused policies and specialized resources requires the legal recognition of Indigenous status. Future studies must broaden their scope beyond the Chittagong Hill Tracts to encompass the varied perspectives of groups residing in the plains.Keywords: Indigenous health, health-seeking behaviour, structural barriers, medical pluralism, Chittagong hill tracts, Bangladesh.1. IntroductionThere are approximately 1.5 to 1.6 million Indigenous people in Bangladesh, which makes up 1-2 percent of the country’s total population. These people primarily reside in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) and some plains regions (IWGIA, 2024; Rahman & Hasan, 2021). Speaking dozens of languages, they are made up of more than 50 different ethnic groups, including the Chakma, Marma, Garo, and others (IWGIA, 2024). They are permanently marginalized: poverty, food insecurity, land insecurity, and bias are prevalent, and health metrics for hill districts fall short of national averages (IWGIA, 2024; Rashid, 2015).Bangladesh has made remarkable strides in health (such as lowering maternal and child mortality), but indigenous people are still isolated and have not seen similar advancements (Rashid, 2015). Known as ”tribal” or ”pahari” (hill) populations, they are not granted any special legal status and frequently face service gaps, cultural insensitivity, and language barriers when seeking care (Rashid, 2015; Rahman & Hasan, 2021).Health-seeking behaviour – the process by which individuals seek out cures for noticed symptoms – is shaped by cultural beliefs, gender standards, socioeconomic level, and system of health factors. For the Indigenous people of Bangladesh, this means medical pluralism (combining traditional and modern treatment) and special barriers for formal facilities. Early ethnography reports a pattern of tribal families putting off or skipping biomedical treatment for older or spirit-based issues (Rahman et al., 2012; Haque et al., 2018). Furthermore, gender roles tend to restrict women’s freedom (men or elders must permit a clinic visit) and determine whether a woman patient can be treated by a male provider (Rahman et al., 2012; Nawaz & Bushra, 2023). Poor health literacy – limited self-knowledge of the cause of diseases and formal treatment – and limited formal education boost adherence to well-known folk treatment (Hossen et al., 2023; Rahman & Hasan, 2021). Geography also casts a long shadow: the CHT and other tribal communities are located well away, in mountainous country with sparse roads, so the time spent getting there and the lack of transport make visits to facilities costly or unaffordable (Hossen et al., 2023; Akter et al., 2019). This narrative review synthesizes the evidence (2000–2024) for health-seeking among indigenous Bangladeshis. We focus on traditional healing, maternal/reproductive care, mental health, nutrition, gender/cultural barriers, health literacy, NGO/community roles, and access to public health systems. We compiled peer-reviewed sources (2000–2024) and credible reports (government/NGO) (≥40 sources), organizing findings into IMRAD format.This analysis highlights one of the main shortcomings of the current research, which is its heavy emphasis on Indigenous groups in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT). The results may therefore not be as generalizable to plains-dwelling people (e.g., Garo, Santal) and are more reflective of hill tribes like as the Chakma and Marma.2. MethodsWe performed a structured literature search of PubMed, Google Scholar, Google, and BanglaJOL for terms like “indigenous health”, “tribal Bangladesh”, “health-seeking behavior”, “health literacy”, “Chittagong Hill Tracts”, and the thematic terms above. In order to get the most recent evidence, the search was carried out in May 2025. Titles and abstracts were used to determine the relevance of the original pool of entries. After that, the complete texts of the remaining sources were evaluated in light of the inclusion requirements. The ultimate selection of 65 sources for thorough analysis and synthesis was the result of this approach.Inclusion criteria were studies or reports (2000–2024) focusing on health practices of Bangladesh’s Indigenous peoples (tribal, Adivasi) or disaggregating data by ethnicity. We prioritized peer-reviewed articles with DOIs, supplemented by government/NGO reports. In total, 65 relevant sources were identified, of which ~30 were primary empirical studies and others were reviews or background sources. Content was extracted on thematic areas and synthesized into a journal-style narrative.3. Results3.1. Traditional and Spiritual Healing PracticesMedical pluralism is widespread. Several studies report that traditional healers (kaviraj, faith healers, shamans) remain primary health-care providers in tribal villages (Rahman et al., 2012; Haque et al., 2018). A qualitative study of rural Bangladesh found “traditional healing was widely practiced as the means of primary healthcare” (especially among poorer households) (Haque et al., 2018). In tribal communities, herbalists and spiritual healers are “still very popular” (Rahman et al., 2012), and entire families often consult a folkloric healer (kabiraji or bhandari ) before or instead of a clinic. Folk practices include herbal remedies, amulets, religious rituals (Kalami, Bhandai), and tribal herbal medicine (Haque et al., 2018). For example, an UNESCO review notes “the majority of the rural and ethnic communities of Bangladesh still rely on the kavirajes for their primary health care”. (UNESCO, 2009)Importantly, many Indigenous patients will use both systems sequentially: they may first try a kabiraji, and if symptoms persist, later visit a doctor. According to studies, even in cases where biomedical care is free, patients may choose to spend more on a healer if they feel heard: perceived ”quality” of treatment (respectful care) can occasionally surpass cost (Rahman et al., 2012). Choice of healer is also influenced by gender roles: women may seek the services of a female spiritual healer for stigmatized conditions (such as gynecological problems or gender-based violence).3.2. Maternal and Reproductive HealthIndigenous women experience notably poor maternal and reproductive outcomes. Bangladesh has seen dramatic MMR declines nationally, but the CHT has “the worst health record in the country” for mothers (Akter et al., 2019). Low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, a major risk factor associated with maternal neglect, are most common in the CHT in Bangladesh, according to UNICEF data (Akter et al., 2019). Tribal women utilize prenatal and skilled delivery services at significantly lower rates than other groups, which reflects deeper care gaps.For example, one CHT survey found only 14% of pregnant tribal women had ≥4 prenatal visits, while 70% had no antenatal care at all (Karim & Kamal, 2020). Only 46% of tribal deliveries were attended by a skilled birth attendant (SBA), compared to ~52% nationally (Karim & Kamal, 2020).Barriers are cultural and structural. Many women expressed a preference for home-based, culturally relevant care (e.g., birthing at home with an older female relative) (Akter et al., 2020). Formal facilities are often seen as for emergencies only. Key obstacles include a lack of awareness about the importance of MHC, costs (even “free” services incur transport and opportunity costs), and language/communication issues with Bengali-speaking staff (Akter et al., 2019). For instance, Akter et al. report that women wanted “culturally relevant, respectful, home-based and affordable care,” and that many perceived clinics as only for complications(Akter et al., 2020). In addition, surveys note that distance to facilities (hilly terrain, poor roads) and service costs (informal fees) deter even motivated women(Akter et al., 2019; Hossen et al., 2023). Some indigenous women fear mistreatment: demands for unofficial payments and reports of abuse by staff were also documented(Akter et al., 2019).Notably, targeted interventions have shown promise. Evaluations of the UNDP-led CHT Development Facility reported increased maternal care usage in intervention areas (Akter et al., 2019). For example, Akter et al. report that more tribal women than before sought prenatal, skilled delivery, and postnatal care in project locations (Akter et al., 2019). This implies that when outreach initiatives and female community health professionals appropriately address cultural demands, uptake can be improved.3.3. Mental HealthMental health care is deeply underserved. Indigenous communities report high stigma: one study found that traditional beliefs still dominate, with many attributing mental illness to evil spirits rather than medical causes (Faruk & Hasan, 2022). In Bangladesh, mental disorders carry heavy stigma, and avoidance is common. For example, Faruk et al. note that “mental illnesses in Bangladesh are generally seen as a consequence of possession of evil spirits” and that stigma leads to low help-seeking.In remote hill areas, professional services are extremely scarce: one country profile notes, “few seek attention from professional services…because in these remote areas few resources are available” (Faruk & Hasan, 2022). In practice, this means few psychiatrists or psychologists serve Indigenous districts. Faruk et al. (2023) highlight that almost no mental health professionals come from Indigenous backgrounds, so even available services often feel alien. Concretely, one analysis attributes poor access partly to“insufficient number of healthcare professionals representing Indigenous communities” .Gender also affects mental health: according to a stigma study conducted among CHT tribes, women reported overall lower awareness of treatment choices and higher levels of stigma than men (Faruk et al., 2023). Prayer and the use of traditional healers for ”possession” are common community coping mechanisms. Finally, limited awareness of mental illness and a lack of culturally competent counseling continue to be major obstacles.3.4. Nutrition and MalnutritionIn both mainstream and Indigenous populations, chronic malnutrition is prevalent. Undernutrition and rising overweight are two burdens highlighted by recent studies. Similar levels of malnutrition were seen in tribal and non-tribal populations in a 2024 survey of schoolchildren, with approximately 15–18% of both groups experiencing stunting or wasting (Karim, 2024). In other words, tribal children’s nutritional status is no better than that of Bengalis. A similar trend can be seen in adult data: according to a PLOS study conducted in northwest Bangladesh, tribal adults showed much lower rates of obesity than non-tribals but comparable rates of undernutrition (Karim et al., 2023). For example, among men, ~9% of tribal men were underweight (vs ~12% of tribal women) with far fewer tribal adults overweight (≈11% vs ≈27–29% in non-tribals) (Karim et al., 2023).However, pockets of severe malnutrition exist: media and NGO reports on tea estate communities (often Garo and Santal) describe “hunger and hardship”, with under-5 stunting rates exceeding 30%. One recent global pediatrics study in a Garo region found 27.98% stunting among under-5s (with ~7.7% also overweight) (Hasan et al., 2025), indicating a coexistence of under- and over-nutrition. Environmental factors contribute: poor sanitation is a key determinant of tribal child growth. A Bangladesh study showed that high rates of open defecation in tribal villages were strongly linked to worse height-for-age scores (Sinharoy et al., 2019).Poor nutrition reflects multiple drivers: food insecurity, poverty, and limited education on diets. Indigenous diets, often based on plantation labor wages or upland farming, can lack diversity. Health services rarely include nutrition counseling. Though beyond the scope of “seeking care,” poor nutrition increases illness risk and thus amplifies health-care needs.3.5. Gender and Cultural BarriersPatriarchy and cultural norms heavily mediate care-seeking. In Indigenous families, men and elders typically control health decisions. Rahman et al. found that “gender and age play a role in making [health] decisions” in tribal households (Rahman et al., 2012). For example, a young tribal woman may require her husband’s or father’s permission to visit a clinic. Female patients also often prefer female providers due to modesty – a huge issue when rural clinics seldom have female doctors.
