records.title: A Special Issue: Coding for Children With Special Health Care Needs
records.authors: Melissa A. Rappo; Peter D. Rappo
records.abstract: This article was written by Peter D. Rappo, MD, FAAP, and Melissa A. Rappo, BA. Dr Peter Rappo is a primary care pediatrician practicing in Brockton, MA. He is a former American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Massachusetts Chapter president, a former chair of the AAP Committee on Practice and Ambulatory Medicine, and an assistant clinical professor of pediatrics at Harvard University School of Medicine. His interest in coding stems from his interest in the care of children with special health care needs. Melissa Rappo has a BA from Boston University and works at the Center for Adolescent Substance Abuse Research at Children's Hospital Boston as a clinician and researcher.A number of sources have indicated that the percentage of children in primary care settings with special health care needs ranges from 1% to 20%. At the extreme low end of this range are children with a variety of technology-dependent issues, including but not limited to ventilator dependence, tube feeding, and requirements for ongoing monitoring and life support. At the upper end of this range are children whose medical conditions (eg, asthma, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, diabetes mellitus) interfere with their activities of daily living. Children with such conditions are twice as likely to be hospitalized as the average child and will spend 4 times as many days in the hospital as children without a chronic medical condition. If one assumes that the costs for provision of preventive care and medical services are $1,000 per year for the average child, a child with a complex illness will have a higher relative cost (eg, a child with spina bifida will have average medical costs 32 times greater than the normal child).Pediatrics is unique in that it has the broadest diagnostic range of any medical specialty and is also noted to have the lowest payment for the provision of medical services of any medical specialty. With this in mind, the capturing of time and effort spent by the pediatrician in caring for children with special health care needs is compelling and critical to the survival of pediatrics as a freestanding discipline.Although the provision of managed care improved access to services for children without chronic illness, global bud-geting and capitation put children with chronic conditions at significant risk for being unable to receive the care they require. Understanding current coding guidelines can ensure that pediatricians receive fair compensation for the additional work required in caring for these patients.Let us begin with coding scenarios that are likely to be used by clinicians under the present system and then continue with options that will enhance the operating efficiencies of a pediatric practice.Preventive care is the hallmark of American pediatrics. Children with special health care needs will be seen for anticipatory guidance, safety counseling, nutritional services, review of development and education, and provision of immunizations in the same way that a child without a disability would. However, it is likely that in addition to performing a preventive medicine service (Current Procedural Terminology [CPT®] codes 99381–99385 for a new patient and 99391–99395 for an established patient) a discussion of the child's chronic condition will ensue. A problem-oriented visit may be reported in addition to the preventive medicine service when an abnormality is encountered or a preexisting problem is addressed and requires additional work to perform the key components. The selection of the evaluation and management (E/M) service will be based on the performance and documentation of the key components (history, physical examination, medical decision-making) required for the type of visit (new versus established patient). When time spent counseling or coordinating care requires more than 50% of the total face-to-face encounter time for the problem-oriented service, the selection of the E/M code may be based on the total time. Time will often be used as the controlling factor in the selection of the problem-oriented visit code because the focus of the additional work is to discuss the child's condition (ie, counseling). To support the additional work performed in association with the problem-oriented visit, separate documentation must be maintained in the medical record. That documentation may be on a separate progress note or, if included on the same progress note, must clearly reflect the additional work performed. When using time as the controlling factor in the selection of the code, the total time spent in counseling and a summary of the discussion issues must be documented. The preventive medicine service code should be linked to International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification code V20.2, routine infant or child health check. The office visit code (99201–99215 with modifier 25 appended) should be linked to the appropriate diagnosis code(s) for the chronic condition(s). Physicians typically emphasize the history and physical examination when determining the level of an E/M encounter. Although this is intrinsic to a visit for a child with special health care needs, medical decision-making becomes a critical factor for the care of children with complex needs. Medical decision-making is based on the complexity of the diagnosis, range of diagnostic possibilities, difficulty in determining a treatment plan and other therapeutic options, and potential for adverse outcomes and vicarious liability (the “beads of sweat” factor). Because this decision-making process is not easily captured in standard documentation formats, it is incumbent on the practitioner to suggest that a range of possibilities was considered and the patient was given instructions that would facilitate a successful therapeutic outcome.To determine the level of medical decision-making for a particular service, 2 of the following 3 elements must be met or exceeded: prolonged services, case management services, and care plan oversight. The Table demonstrates how the level of medical decision-making should be determined.Children with special health care needs will often require prolonged services with direct (face-to-face) or non–face-to-face patient contact. For example, a child newly diagnosed with cystic fibrosis is seen for initiation of a treatment plan. A detailed history and physical examination are performed. The physician then spends an additional 60 minutes reviewing the treatment plan, diet, prognosis, and need for compliance and ongoing care with the parents. A total of 80 minutes is spent face to face with the patient or parents. This visit would be reported with established office visit code 99214, detailed history and physical examination with moderate to high medical decision-making, and 99354, prolonged physician service in the office, first hour. Prolonged physician service with face-to-face patient contact may be reported in the outpatient or inpatient setting. Codes 99354, prolonged services in office or outpatient setting, and 99356, prolonged services in the inpatient setting, are reported for the first hour of prolonged care. Codes 99355, office or outpatient setting, and 99357, inpatient setting, are reported for each additional 30 minutes of prolonged service.Children with chronic illness may present to the practitioner with extensive medical records, school evaluations, or consultant assessments that need to be reviewed. Subsequent communication or coordination with other professionals may be required. Prolonged physician service without direct (face-to-face) patient contact may be appropriate in these cases. Codes 99358 and 99359 are used to report the total duration of non–face-to-face time spent by a physician on a given date before or after direct (face-to-face) patient care is provided. Code 99358 is reported for the first 30 to 74 minutes of non–face-to-face prolonged service, and 99359 may be reported for each subsequent 30 minutes spent providing the service.Prolonged service codes are add-on codes, meaning that they are reported in addition to the office/outpatient or inpatient E/M service. The first 30 minutes of prolonged service cannot be reported because it is considered to be part of the work performed in the E/M service. Prolonged service of less than 15 minutes beyond the first hour or beyond the final 30 minutes cannot be reported. The time does not need to be continuous and because these are time-based services, the total time spent must be documented in the medical record.At times it may be necessary to schedule a medical conference with a variety of health care professionals to determine an appropriate treatment course for an individual child with complex illness. The patient will usually not be present at such a meeting. CPT code 99361 is used to report a medical conference lasting approximately 30 minutes by a physician with an interdisciplinary team of health professionals or representatives of community agencies to coordinate activities of patient care. A medical conference lasting approximately 60 minutes is reported with code 99362. Although the physician may schedule such a conference at his or her office, there is no requirement that it only be scheduled at the practitioner's office. Other appropriate settings might be at a school, hospital, or long-term care setting.CPT codes are available to report telephone management, but payers have been resistant to assign a relative value for the codes (99371–99373) because of difficulty with determining levels of service, challenges around documentation, and concern about potential for abuse. However, caring for children with special health care needs will generate significant telephone traffic and engender telephone conversations that can be complex and beneficial to the child's family. The AAP Section on Telephone Care is creating a working document to assist practitioners with capturing the time and effort spent in telephone management. Telephone management time is bundled into each E/M code as part of preservice and post-service. For example, code 99213 includes 11 minutes of time that is intrinsic to this code. Because of the complexity of this issue, pediatricians continue to struggle to be fairly reimbursed for time spent on the telephone.The potential Rosetta stone for capturing time spent on the telephone and in performing other case management activities is included in care plan oversight services. The importance of these codes becomes obvious when one considers the range of communications that a physician undertakes when caring for a child with chronic illness. Although time spent coordinating care on the telephone is most obvious, one must consider the review of consultative letters, educational plans, care plans, and new laboratory and diagnostic evaluations and dealing with change in fax orders. The challenge, of course, is to document these myriad encounters and track the time spent on these activities.Care plan oversight codes are used to report recurrent physician supervision (non–face-to-face) of a patient who requires multidisciplinary care and ongoing physician involvement. Only the physician who has the predominant supervisory role in the care of the patient or is the sole provider of services to the patient may report these codes.Care plan oversight services include regular development, revision, and oversight of treatment care plans; care coordination activities via telephone or team conferences with the family or other caregivers; care coordination activities with other medical professionals; oversight of the patient's work or school programs that require medical supervision; and review of laboratory results, diagnostic studies, and patient status reports.These services are not reported when furnished by incident-to staff, when associated with a face-to-face E/M service (eg, interpretation of diagnostic study), or with very low-intensity or infrequent supervisory services that are included in the pre- and post-encounter work for an E/M service. Any time spent on care plan oversight activities that are separately reported with other CPT codes (eg, 99371– 99373 for telephone calls) cannot be used in the determination of the time.Care plan oversight services are reported based on the total time spent within a calendar month. Code 99374 is used to report 15 to 29 minutes of physician supervision of a patient under the care of a home health care agency; 99375 is reported when 30 minutes or more is spent performing the services. Similarly, there are time-based codes for physician supervision of patients in hospice care (99377–99378) and a nursing facility (99379–99380). Of particular relevance are individual codes with identical time requirements for patients primarily cared for at home who are not under the care of a home health agency. Code 99339 is reported when 15 to 29 minutes per month is spent providing the services; code 99340 is reported for 30 minutes or more per month.The Care Plan Oversight Encounter Worksheet is a useful tool that helps to define the various possible encounters and document the time spent on each individual activity. Although the template is a very useful device, it will require the busy practitioner to remember to use it.Not mentioned previously is the use of an online E/M service. At this time, there is no uniformity around use of electronic messaging with patients and payment by insurers for the provision of this service. Patients are enthusiastic about communicating with their physicians electronically, but in a national survey conducted by Forrester Research, they were only willing to pay $3 for each encounter. However, insurers are embracing the concept of electronic messaging for follow-up and management of one select group of their insureds—patients with chronic illness.Code 0074T (a Category III CPT code) includes the physician's personal response to a patient's online inquiry via the Internet or similar electronic communications network. There must be permanent storage of the response (electronic or hard copy of the encounter). The intent of this code is to include the total interchange of online inquiries and other communications associated with a single patient encounter or inquiry. Also, guidelines clarify that code 0074T is not intended to be reported for patient services considered to be part of the work before and after other services.Some patients are so medically complex that transportation to a pediatric facility may cause significant disruption to office flow and routine. Therefore, a home visit (that medical tradition of a former era) would be appropriate. In most cases, use of home visits is for well care and the provision of immunizations to children with technology or ventilator dependence. Because an age-appropriate comprehensive history and physical examination are done as part of the well examination and the further discussions of medical decision-making are complex, it may be appropriate to report the established patient preventive medicine visit services (99391–99395) with a problem-oriented visit (99348–99349 with modifier 25) based on counseling time or the level of history and medical decision-making performed that was related to the abnormality or condition(s). The level of service reported for home visits must be based on 2 of the 3 key components or time if more than 50% of the face-to-face encounter is spent in counseling or coordination of care. These services would be reported with place of service code 12 (home). Any procedures (eg, vaccines, administration of vaccines, venipuncture, capillary stick) should also be reported using the same place of service.Health and behavior assessment codes are available when providing services for those patients who have medical conditions that may or will benefit from psychosocial interventions. These codes are not used for preventive medicine counseling and risk-factor reduction interventions and cannot be reported on the same day as another E/M service performed by the same physician. They are not used by physicians and are not applicable for services provided to patients because of a psychiatric condition.These codes are significant only to those physicians who practice in states where insurers allow nonphysician providers (eg, social workers, licensed therapists, psychologists, trained nurses) to bill for their services independently or as incident to those provided by the physician. Code 96150 is reported for each 15 minutes of face-to-face time with the patient to perform an initial health and behavior assessment. Code 96151 is reported for a reassessment. Health and behavior intervention is reported with codes 99152–99155. When intervention is provided to an individual, the services are reported with code 96152 (each 15 minutes). When reporting intervention provided to a group of patients, use code 96153. Code 96154 is used to report a family intervention when the patient is present; code 96155 is reported for a family intervention when the patient is absent. Clearly, a practice that has a large number of children with similar chronic illnesses may well find that there is an economy of scale in providing these behavioral health interventions in a group format.If a practitioner has created a training curriculum for educating patients on management of their medical condition, he or she may employ a nonphysician health care professional to provide education using a standardized curriculum for patients with that disease. The curriculum may be modified as necessary based on the patient's clinical needs or the patient or caregiver's cultural norms and health literacy. These services are used to teach the patient or caregiver how to effectively manage the illness(es) or condition(s) or delay disease comorbidity(ies) in conjunction with the professional health care team. They are reported based on the total face-to-face time (each 30 minutes) and the number of patients receiving the education and training. CPT code 98960 is reported for each 30 minutes of education and training provided to an individual patient; code98961 is reported when they are provided to 2 to 4 patients; and code 98962 is reported when 5 to 8 patients receive them. For example, if a physician has a large number of asthmatic patients in the practice, the use of a standardized curriculum emphasizing the importance of peak flow monitoring, use of preventive medications, and avoidance of overuse of rescue medications should improve patient compliance and safety for this chronic illness.Children with chronic illness who have technology dependence may require adjustment of their various technological interventions. For example, code 43752 is reported for placement of a nasogastric tube by the physician; code 43760 is reported when changing a gastrostomy tube; and code 43761 is reported when repositioning the gastric feeding tube. Other commonly performed procedures include insertion of a non-indwelling bladder catheter (51701) or an indwelling catheter (51702). For the patient with chronic respiratory disease, code 94760, pulse oximetry, may be reported for monitoring of oxygen saturation. If multiple determinations are required as in the case of monitoring during status asthmaticus, report code 94761. Spirometry is reported with code 94010, and nebulizer therapy should be reported with code 94640. If multiple nebulizations are required on the same visit, modifier 76 would be appended to 94640 (if required by the payer). Don't forget the new codes to report home apnea monitoring when appropriate. Physicians will report their services with codes 94774 (pediatric home apnea monitoring event recording including respiratory rate, pattern, and heart rate per 30-day period of time; includes monitor attachment, download of data, physician review and interpretation, and preparation of a report) or 94777 (physician review, interpretation, and preparation of report only).Although a variety of coding options exist for managing patients with chronic illness, there may not be uniformity among payers in recognizing all of the listed codes. In most states, physicians have the option of billing a patient for services that are not covered under a patient's health plan. Many insurers are silent on the issue of provision of payment for telephone time or electronic messaging. records.title: Maintaining Privacy and Security in Cyberspace
records.authors: Maureen McDermott; Jennifer Lyn Reeves; Gabriela Mendez
records.abstract: You’ve been hacked!This cataclysmic message heralded from cyberspace incites panic in the minds and wallets of people around the world. These ubiquitous data breaches occur frequently to seemingly innocuous targets. A breach occurs when a cyberhacker physically gains access to files on a computer or remotely bypasses a network’s security system, gaining access to data, and stealing sensitive information. Remote network security breaches are a common method for taking sensitive information from companies. The confidential information can then be sold on the deep web market, used to steal identities to open up fake credit card accounts, or to blackmail an individual or group (TrendMicro, 2018).The first data breach of 2019 was reported fewer than 24 hours into the new year (Targett, 2019). Large corporations dominate the news concerning incurred security breaches that expose customers’ personal details and financial resources. Recent examples (Targett, 2019) include Facebook (up to 2 billion accounts compromised), the Marriott Hotel chain (over 500 million accounts hacked), and Under Armour (about 150 million accounts jeopardized. Additionally, Equifax, one of three major credit reporting agencies whose databases contain susceptible personal information such as Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, and so forth, was hacked in 2017. The breach affected 143 million U.S. consumers and extended to the United Kingdom with a total of 400,000 U.K. customers affected (TrendMicro, 2018). Quite possibly the largest data breach of all time occurred in January 2019 involving a collection of 773 million unique emails and 21,222,975 unique passwords from thousands of different users onto the deep web (Davis, 2019).This episodic hacking obliges users to be habitually cognizant that their financial information is vulnerable and could end up being shared with unintended recipients. Future breaches are predicted to be even more creative and impactful, focusing in on biometrics, mobile phones, cloudbased storage, and gamers (Bayern, 2018). Forbes contributor Kyle Torpey (2019) attributes this seemingly endless cycle of data breaches to the consumer’s desire for convenience overriding concerns about security, and the willingness of malicious hackers waiting for these opportunities.Data breaches are not a new phenomenon; breaches of paper records in the United States have been traced back almost 70 years. According to Solove (2004), most centralized record keeping at the national level in the United States was done on paper for the Census. In the 1950s, the Social Security Administration of the U.S. government assigned citizens nine digit numbers and required stringent reporting and record keeping of income. Records were computerized and stored in huge databases, and Social Security numbers eventually became useful identifiers in the private sector (e.g., by banks and credit card companies) and as student numbers for colleges and universities. In the 1970s, the U.S. government began selling batches of census data stored on magnetic tapes to marketing companies, but supplied physical addresses and not names to protect privacy (Solove, 2004). This trend of “number instead of name” was the genesis of identity theft thus compromising the “digital dossier” in the early 1980s. However, the invasion of the digital dossier did not pervade tech jargon rapidly. It reemerged as “digital footprint” during the time when the term “carbon footprint” pervaded mass media. In the mid 1990s, commercial companies and private individuals transformed websites into cyberspace shopping experiences, thus opening the Internet information superhighway for business and cybercrime (Sommer, 1998).With these recent revelations of breaches involving social media applications, privacy and security concerns have emerged for administrators, faculty, staff, students, and parents. Academia is far from safe as there has been noted cases of hacking and data loss. In March of 2019, private colleges Grinnell, Hamilton, and Oberlin reported breaches (Smith, 2019). Grinnell and Hamilton reported that applicants received emails from someone who claimed to have unauthorized access to their database containing personally identifiable information. These emails, which came from official college addresses, offered to sell them their completed admission file which included comments from admissions officers and tentative decisions (M. Smith, 2019). A spokesperson from Oberlin said their applicants and students who enrolled during or after the fall of 2014 did not receive emails like the ones at Grinnell and Hamilton; however, their names, addresses, birthdays, emails, and Social Security numbers were possibly exposed. Oberlin suggested that fraud alerts should be added to victim’s credit card reports. All three colleges use software system Slate to manage this information, and all three colleges reported this breach to Slate and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Smith, 2019).In 2010, the Social Security numbers of 43,000 Yale affiliates became publicly available on Google because they had been stored on servers that were also used to hold open-source materials (Fuchs, 2018). In July 2018, Yale notified about 119,000 faculty, staff, and alumni that their names and Social Security numbers had been compromised between the years of 2008 and 2009. This breach also compromised some of the victims’ dates of birth, physical addresses, and email addresses. The breach occurred in September 2011 when the university was clearing out unnecessary personal data, and was not discovered by Yale until June 2018. Yale offered to pay expenses for 12 months of identity-monitoring services for victims of both breaches (Fuchs, 2018). According to Mariwala and McCooey (2018), two class action lawsuits have been filed against Yale alleging negligence; unfair trade practices; and reckless, wanton, and willful misconduct. Plaintiffs are requesting further compensatory and punitive damages.Data breaches have also invaded the privacy of students in PK–12 school districts. The San Diego School District reported a large data breach where data including Social Security numbers from as many as 500,000 students were compromised and possibly stolen (Luke & Stuckney, 2018). The Hoopeston, Illinois Area School District’s website was compromised when families received repeated false and outrageous voicemail messages at 3 A.M. No student data were taken; however, this demonstrates the vulnerability that exists in the technology age (Francis, 2018).Even though parents may be able to monitor what educational apps their children use at home, they have little input about what happens at school. The Electronic Freedom Foundation, a nonprofit organization that defends digital privacy, free speech, and innovation, identified school-issued devices and education technology platforms as the most vulnerable for data breaches. For these reasons, parents should be asked for consent or given the option to opt-out of education technology.On December 1, 2015, the Electronic Frontier Foundation filed a lawsuit against Google for data mining student’s personal information and internet search histories in Google Apps for Education and Google Chromebook (Alim, Cardozo, Gebhart, Gullo, & Kalia, 2017). Between December 15, 2015 and January 2017, the Electronic Frontier Foundation posted a survey about student privacy on their website and disseminated links on their other social media sources. Over 1,000 responses from students, parents, teachers, and administrators were compiled into the report “Spying on Students” (Alim et al., 2017). It raised concerns about technology usage that tracks online student’s behavior before they are old enough to understand the implications of digital footprints, privacy, and security and addressed issues of federal law, state law, and industry self regulation.One legal measure is the federal law Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act which requires technology providers to acquire parental consent before collecting student’s personal information. Enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, this law includes consent requirements for technology providers that are utilizing student data for anything other than disclosed to the school district. Verifiable parental consent is required for any collection of identifiable student information for students younger than 13. The Federal Trade Commission also offers a Student Privacy Pledge voluntarily signed by ed tech companies, but the Electronic Frontier Foundation identified glaring loopholes in what constitutes student information (Alim et al., 2017).Resulting from increased technology integration in brick and mortar classrooms and the pervasiveness of distance education, the International Society for Technology in Education asserts that educators who use applications to engage students must “Model and promote management of personal data and digital identity and protect student data privacy” (International Society for Technology in Education, 2017, para. 3). International Society for Technology in Education (2019) encourages the development of digital citizens who critically evaluate online information and create positive online footprints.Ironically, while digital citizens harness technology for the benefit of communities, hackers simultaneously undermine these efforts for their own selfish gains. These violations demonstrate the need for curricular work and professional development for faculty and staff (with support from the administration) in the areas of digital footprints and evaluation of websites for security and privacy.According to Dennen (2015), digital footprints can be likened to physical footprints rendered unique to their owners, and contain the information users leave behind on the Internet resulting from online activity. There are two kinds of digital footprints— active and passive. A passive digital footprint is a data trail users unintentionally leave online. When connecting to the Internet, websites detect IP addresses and locations and download cookies, and search engines save users’ histories automatically with no detection. In the past few years, many websites have eliminated this potential for passive footprints by adding pop-up boxes that ask users to read the terms of service and acknowledge agreement by simply checking a box before entering the site (McDermott, 2018).Active footprints, on the other hand, refer to the data trail users know they are leaving—including signing into social media sites such as Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, Pinterest, Instagram, Snapchat, and various educational learning management systems such as Google Classroom, Canvas, and Blackboard. Even “liking” pages, posts, or photos on social media or commenting with an icon to a classmate’s discussion board posting contributes to a user’s digital footprint.These active footprints generate when users retrieve email for work and school, as well as when accessing company websites and learning management systems. Regardless of whether digital footprints are active or passive, privacy and security are areas for concern. Although privacy and security are not synonymous, what they have in common is that people don’t usually know there is a problem until it has happened already and is broadcast over the news (McDermott, Reeves, Capo, Mendez, & Karp, 2019). Even when users select the most stringent privacy options involving how their data are displayed, stored, used, and shared—this does not guarantee security from data hackers. Security involves how companies protect information users agree to share, so when something is hacked both security and privacy are compromised.Before generating digital footprints, consumers and educators should understand a company’s security policy. According to Smith (2018), one of the strongest security indicators of a website is the first few letters on the browser address bar. Early website addresses started with HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP), the procedure that allowed network administrators to share information. Unfortunately, intercepting the information was almost as simple as it was to share it, so an encryption encoding system was developed called HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS). Computers using HTTPS send and receive messages through the Secure Sockets Layer or the Transport Layer Security protocol which validates security certificates (Sheldon, 2017). Both Sheldon (2017) and P. Smith (2018) recommend consumers verify five important things prior to its use: (a) authentication and authorization with multifactor identification, (b) strong passwords that contain at least one uppercase letter and a numerical character, (c) email confirmation when an account is opened, (d) frequent password changes, and (e) sign-in requirements for each session.In addition to the steps above, consumers should also check Breach Level Index which is a dynamic website that invites users from around the world to report/document security breaches. An analysis of data breaches by type was documented from spring 2013 through 2018. Identity theft has topped the number of breach incidents since 2013. In 2018 there were 957 incidents of identity theft, followed by approximately 212 incidents of financial access breaches and 211 incidences of account access breaches (Data breach statistics, 2019). Malicious outsiders were responsible for more than half of all breaches in 2018, followed by accidental loss. When looking at the loss by industry, social media accounts for more than half of the industry breaches in 2018 with 2,739,445,349 records stolen (Data breach statistics, 2019). Breach Line also reported that education had the second lowest number of data breaches at 0.27%; however, this still includes 12,984,701 compromised records in 2018 alone!Sheldon (2017) reported that the highest threats to mobile app security come from broken cryptography, unintended data leakage, weak server side controls, client side injection, and poor authorization and authentication. P. Smith (2018) suggested making good choices in regard to safety such as not disclosing too much online, not accepting friend requests or personal messages from strangers, and blocking people who write or display inappropriate things. When evaluating for security, users should investigate if websites scan for robots. There are many types of “bots” which scan websites that save the contents of every page in the search index. Bots can also be detected when users share networks with others on proxy services, work or school networks, virtual private networks, and websites such as Amazon, EC2, and Google App Engine. Chat bots monitor for appropriate language and “chatterbots” respond to messages appearing to be an actual person. However, some bots contain malware that raid email address books to link them to spam mailing lists. Other bots raid entire computer systems, duplicate content, and then infect them with viruses (Christensson, 2014).The security section from Pinterest (2019) entitled “We protected your account” provides examples of some security concepts users should know. It advises users to save Pins from original sources, and use full links instead of using a redirect like bit.ly or other link shorteners. Pinterest’s security features enable account blocking when it detects a bot or if users do one or any of the following: log in frequently, comment or save Pins quickly, and follow several people rapidly.Additionally, Pinterest’s first requirement compels users to verify they are at least 13. Other security tips (from their website) include activating two-factor authentication, connecting the account to Google or Facebook, verifying current email, and changing passwords regularly. Pinterest also retains the rights to suspend accounts if they believe users have violated the website’s acceptable use policy. Pinterest also has a user-friendly contact page if users have been blocked and not restored within 24 hours.Before generating digital footprints, users should also be aware of a company’s privacy policies to protect personal information and learn how the company uses the data it collects (McDermott, 2018). The privacy statement should be dated and current and address how users communicate with each other, what details users can see about each other, and if data will be shared with third parties.Typically, school and evaluate applications, and software for educational in parents and to understand how to evaluate the privacy and security of apps and there are educators can use to address this useful to evaluate privacy policies and is (2017) of individuals should use to evaluate privacy policies personal The address such as of terms to data and rights and legal also recommend about companies with which personal data will be whether these companies are from using or selling data, and the for of Education Privacy of (2019) offers for using applications in the This of privacy using and apps by the school given that school need to evaluate the for privacy and security prior to also include a of to individuals evaluate whether apps and other online protect information. records.title: The Other Jack Tanner: Shaw and Robert Loraine
records.abstract: Robert Loraine, whose biography has preoccupied Lanayre D. Liggera for many years, was born into a theatrical family. Apprenticed to the stage from an early age, he was in London by the 1890s, and, in the early years of the new century, was trying his luck in the United States, hoping to find an avenue to fame and fortune.Loraine knew something of Bernard Shaw, having drawn a favorable mention from the sometime theater critic. Aware that the critic was also a playwright, whose plays had been published if rarely performed, he had arranged to have Shaw's plays sent to him as and when they might appear in print, which is how he came to have a copy of Man and Superman. As he read it, on a train from Boston to New York, he realized that this was the discovery that had hitherto eluded him. “Whether I cried Eureka or no,” he later wrote, “I knew at once this was a marvellous play—simply bound to succeed in the theatre—and danced a jig of delight up and down the corridor of the train, elated beyond bounds by the brilliance of the book itself, and rejoicing at the prospect of producing and acting in a masterpiece.” Loraine's eureka moment came in the nick of time. He had spent two years searching without finding anything that matched his ambition, and he was seriously considering giving up acting altogether.Convinced that he had at last found the vehicle that would make his name, Loraine set about obtaining the American rights to the play. Having secured them (for a down payment of two hundred pounds against 10 percent of the eventual gross receipts), he sought an American manager to back him, but without success. He then arranged to meet Shaw and secure his cooperation, and was able to do this when, back in London, he attended the matinee performance of Man and Superman at the Court Theatre on 6 June 1905. He was promptly invited to lunch the next day at Adelphi Terrace to discuss his plans. And he also found his backer, the producer Charles Frohman, who had seen the play at the Court ahead of Loraine's arrival in London, and was seeking the owner of the American rights.Loraine claims that Shaw gave him carte blanche to produce Man and Superman in New York. In her exhaustive account of Loraine's life, Liggera says that he received a marked up copy of the play from Shaw. This was presumably a duplicate of the Court promptbook, with the changes necessitated to account for the omission of the third act, and also the deletion of the lengthy dialogue in the first between Tanner and Ann concerning “the birth of the moral passion,” as Shaw described it. Loraine, however, had no intention at all of reproducing the Court production, and Channing Pollock writes in a memoir that he spent part of 1905 preparing the script for Loraine's staging of the play. In particular, Loraine saw Tanner quite differently from Granville Barker (and Shaw). Indeed, he was surely obliged to see him differently. At the Court, Granville Barker had been made up with a prominent red beard to look like Shaw himself, and perhaps thereby to give the character a more forceful presence. But this local allusion would not have been recognized by a New York audience. Loraine's Tanner would be impetuous, vigorous, and comic, where Barker's was subtly witty and thoughtful.Shaw gave a summary account of the difference between the two Tanners in one of his contributions to Winifred Loraine's 1938 biography of her erstwhile husband, which has been mined diligently by Liggera. He found Loraine to be “perfection throughout the first half while Tanner is victorious and irresistible. But when Ann's turn came and Tanner went down to defeat and despair at her hands—this part had been performed to Shaw's complete satisfaction by Harley Granville-Barker—Robert simply would not give in.”However, there was much more that differentiated Loraine's production than his approach to Tanner. He conceived the play as a star vehicle with spectacular settings and effects. The first act was reset in an elegant Virginia mansion, with a veranda, rather than in Roebuck Ramsden's Victorian library in London, with its iconic busts. Most spectacularly, the second act was dominated by a flashy motorcar, in which of course Loraine drove off at the end of the act. Liggera has rescued a photograph of what appears to be the last act replete with an elaborate network of paths and steps, affording a variety of vantage points.Loraine's production was a tremendous success, by far the biggest for any Shaw play up to that point and for a long time in the future. Following its New York run, and the American tour that followed, a remarkable sequence of some 250 performances in all, Loraine returned to London to perform Tanner at the Court. This opportunity had arisen because Barker was busy preparing for his future when the Vedrenne-Barker management shut up shop at the Court, in the throes of writing a new play, Waste, and contemplating the possibility of going to New York where a so-called New Theatre was under consideration. Shaw favored this idea: “There is a tide in the affairs of men, as our national bard has well observed,” he told Barker.Liggera calls the Man and Superman revival at the Court—with Loraine, absent the Shavian beard, in place of Barker—a new production. The novelty was Loraine. For the rest, the settings and most of the supporting cast were the established Court production, into which Loraine had to be fitted.Shaw's favorable description of Loraine's Tanner was not of the New York performance of course, which he never saw, but rather what he elicited for the Court revival, and therefore much of Shaw's own making. This is clear from a lengthy letter he sent to Barker, describing how Loraine had been accommodated, or not, at the Court, which, Shaw told Barker, Loraine “loathed.” “Loraine, who always starts a Company by sacking at least three members of it after the first rehearsal to intimidate the rest, is aghast, and has impulses, which recur at intervals of ten minutes, to take the next boat back to America and leave you to play Tanner.” Shaw claimed to have “assimilated all of his business that is to the good” and “utterly rejected the starry part of it.” For example, in act 2, Loraine had wanted to place the car in the middle of the stage, as he had in New York. Setting it like this would enable him “to deliver the great speech about the tyranny of mothers enthroned in the motor car, with Lillah [McCarthy] somewhere under the wheels with her back to the audience.” Shaw continues, “I immediately saw the value of the idea, and put Lillah in the car in a fascinating attitude with her breast on the driving wheel and Loraine ranting about on the gravel…. [H]is dismay imparts an invaluable quality of earnestness to his acting. He feels that he is on the brink of catastrophe, which is exactly what one wants from Tanner.” Shaw was not, however, able to overcome the difficulties posed by Loraine's refusal to give in to McCarthy's Ann, and she was evidently discomfited by his attitude to her. “It is clear to me that he has never had an Ann to give himself in to,” Shaw wrote to Barker. What's more, and perhaps understandably, as Shaw later told Edith Evans, “Lillah hated him.” Shaw, however, looking to the future, extolled Loraine's qualities, telling Barker he was “far and away the best alternative to yourself that we have been able to find,” and so he cultivated his friendship.There remained one important production at the Court before the Vedrenne-Barker management there closed. This was the first performance of the “Don Juan in Hell” scene, given for a handful of matinees, in which Loraine played Juan, a performance that greatly enhanced his reputation. Granville Barker's secretary, Allan Wade, who had been critical of Loraine as Tanner (“his method … seemed to me to consist in charging at the part, head down, as if he were taking part in a rough football game”) made a particularly acute observation about his Juan. The part, as Wade said, calls for “an astonishing feat of memory.” To accomplish it, he revealed, Loraine had rehearsed Juan with the assistant stage manager every day that he had a performance to give. Wade makes the point that this was because he was now playing a “long and difficult part with which he was unfamiliar,” quite the opposite of his Tanner.Man and Superman became Robert Loraine's talisman, and he revived the play several times, both in London and on tour in the United States, as well as once more in New York. He performed Tanner for the last time in 1932.Loraine was cast in other Shavian roles in London in the years leading up to World War I. In Getting Married, he played St. John Hotchkiss. Liggera says, somewhat dismissively, that this was the first time Loraine had portrayed an unpleasant character. Nevertheless, Hotchkiss is “first cousin” to other young Shavian men, like Tanner, Valentine, and Charteris, as Desmond MacCarthy pointed out long ago. “Perhaps I should not have understood, though I should certainly have enjoyed him,” MacCarthy wrote, “if I had not known his relations.” Charteris, in The Philanderer, was a role that attracted Loraine, and one for which Shaw thought him well suited, although, in the end, not one he ever played. He did, however, play Bluntschli in Arms and the Man, and revived it after the war, when it had a markedly different effect on audiences.There were also roles which he might have played but didn't. One such was John Tarleton in Misalliance. Both Liggera and Stanley Weintraub (in his foreword to her book) take note of a balloon excursion undertaken by Shaw, Loraine, Barker, and Shaw's sister-in-law in 1906. “This historic trip would give Shaw the information to write Misalliance,” Liggera writes. This is simply nonsense. Misalliance was not written until 1909, and became Shaw's contribution to the repertory experiment at the Duke of York's Theatre. It drew on a diverse array of sources, but there is no balloon excursion in the play. It is true that there is an aviator, and that, by the time Shaw came to write it, Loraine had developed an avid interest in flying. The second act of Misalliance—not the play itself, as Weintraub mistakenly suggests—begins with the arrival from his crashed plane of Joey Percival, who, like Loraine, is interested in breaking aviation speed and distance records. It is the case that the first name of one of the brothers whose company supplied the balloon for the 1906 excursion was Percival, but this is a tenuous connection at best.In 1909, just as Loraine's interest in taking to the skies was stirring, he played Mitchener in Shaw's one-act suffragette squib Press Cuttings. Since the Lord Chamberlain had refused a license on the grounds that the characters' names, Balsquith as well as Mitchener, were too easily identified with actual politicians and generals, the performance, which was given twice only at the Court, was announced as a “Private Reception,” and there was no charge for admission, a recognized way of evading the censorship.Of the parts Loraine might have played but didn't, the most interesting, surely, is Henry Higgins. In 1913, having given up flying and once more back in America hoping to restore his damaged finances, Loraine told a reporter (a clipping that has apparently eluded Liggera's well-filled net) that Shaw was writing a new play for him. This can only have been Pygmalion, and indeed there is ample evidence that Shaw wanted Loraine for Higgins, another Shavian character trailing aspects of Loraine's own personality. In the event, however, he did not create Higgins because Mrs. Patrick Campbell, who had already had to work with Loraine, told Shaw he must choose between them: he could not have both. Relying on Margot Peters's biography of Campbell, Liggera quotes from letters between Shaw and Mrs. Pat, but both she and Peters miss Shaw's comment to Barker: “she dreads [him] as he dreaded Lillah—ha! ha! Nemesis!”What makes Loraine a particularly interesting biographical subject is that he was not merely an actor. Indeed, when he took up flying he rapidly attained a reputation as a flier to match, and enhance, his stage fame. He expended a quantity of his theatrical earnings on his aeronautical reputation. The same spirit of adventure carried him into the military in both the Boer War and World War I. Liggera's sources enable her to give a fairly full account of his experiences in both conflicts, as well as of his flying career.After World War I, in which Loraine was seriously wounded, he returned to the stage. He had some success at first, perhaps because he was seen as a war hero. He mounted a notable production of Cyrano de Bergerac—an eminent star vehicle that Loraine had had his eye on since before the war. Indeed, it might be said that panache was a defining characteristic of his stage personality. He now surrounded himself with actors who were veterans of the war. He also revived Arms and the Man, which, as he pointed out to a journalist, played rather differently following the slaughter of 1914–18.Despite a severely damaged leg, Loraine continued to appear on stage, and to do so without exhibiting any physical limitation. Shaw went to see him in Cyrano, and noticed that there was no trace of a handicap in his performance. But when he met Loraine afterward, and they walked away from the theater together, the limp was pronounced and Loraine needed a cane. Violet Vanbrugh reports Loraine's response to Shaw's enquiry about this: “The footlights make me another man. I have no disabilities on the stage except any assumed for the character I am playing.”It may have been the fact that Shaw devoted his 1925 Nobel Prize money to a foundation for the translation of Swedish plays into English that drew Loraine's attention to what would be his final major theatrical achievement: Strindberg's The Father. Strindberg's translator and biographer, Michael Meyer, made an acute and penetrating comment about Loraine's effectiveness as the tormented father. It was no coincidence, he wrote in 1975, that Loraine was one of only two actors to have thus far fully succeeded in Strindberg in Britain, and this was because he was an actor “of a most un-English, one might almost say continental vehemence … and consequently … difficult to cast in roles of ordinary human dimensions.”The last decade of Loraine's career was marked by difficulties, personal as well as professional, and his health was vulnerable. He played no new Shaw roles; the only one left to him, after the postwar Bluntschli, was —Tanner. He clung to the hope of a revival of Man and Superman. A plan for him to spearhead a campaign to spread Shaw's fame in Australia lingered but came to nothing. There were discussions of a an American première of the full four-act version of Superman, but they too came to nothing, chiefly, it seems, because the Theatre Guild, which had a virtual monopoly over productions of Shaw's plays in New York, thought Loraine “too old” for Tanner. He was fifty-six when he managed a comeback, starring in Superman for the last time, in Newport, Rhode Island, in the summer of 1932. Notwithstanding the Great Depression, there was still money in Newport. Liggera cites a perceptive review from the Newport Times: “Mr. Loraine's diction is something to be admired…. There are passages in the play which call for long expressions of opinion from the leading character, and he gave them with a skill which only a master has…. He carried the action forward in a manner which kept the audience sharply alert, and the heavy applause which greeted him was truly deserved.”Lanayre Liggera has devoted half a lifetime to Robert Loraine's diverse career. She has drawn on an enormous quantity of information, ranging from actors' autobiographies and university archives to clippings files, correspondence with actors (such as Evans and John Gielgud, who knew Loraine), and numerous conversations with Robert Loraine's daughter Joan, who gave her access to family papers—and she has had the assistance of Dan Laurence and Stanley Weintraub. She seems never to have found a fact that she doesn't want to share with us, and for this alone her book will be appreciated. The story she tells is certainly fascinating. Nevertheless, her irritation with Shaw sometimes shows. Her accounts of Loraine's aviation exploits and of his service in World War I are thorough.Sad to report, the text of this publication is seriously disfigured by a quantity of errors. Arms and the Man was not first produced in 1874 nor The Devil's Disciple in 1879. Jack Tanner's pamphlet is not titled “The Revisionist's Handbook.” The Mecca of English cricket is Lord's cricket ground, not “a lord's cricket ground.” Robert Falcon Scott was not a lord, although he would no doubt have been knighted, as other members of his ill-fated expedition were, had he not perished on the return journey from the South Pole. records.title: How investors account for the quick and the dead
records.abstract: Poor Ophelia. Gone too soon from the living but now judged harshly for the manner of her departure. What did she do? Was it suicide or an accidental drowning? It mattered for the kind of Christian burial that could be made available to her. (She was, after all, strange, so self-slaughter would come as no surprise.) In Shakespeare's Hamlet, her brother Laertes leaps into her grave, imploring the gravediggers to pile their dirt on both the quick (him, her living brother) and the dead. Of course, it would not be done. These bodies, like so many accounts, were not permitted to mix. In that moment, the social constraints on Laertes and the gravediggers manifested themselves with clarity, revealing “the complex and dynamic configuration of social, economic, and political relations on which [ritual, death, or even] money depends” (Dodd, 2017, p. 244). His choice was not his alone to make (Bandelj, 2012; Zelizer, 1985, 1994, 2012). We are left with the image of an unsalvageable investment now driven, mercilessly, into the ground. Since the publication of Pricing the Priceless Child, sociologists have examined the critical passage from one life stage to another. What is allowed and what cannot be mixed in response to a child's death, Zelizer asked. How does the death of a child differ from that of an adult? How do we express these differences meaningfully through our monies? Unlike Ophelia, the dead in Pricing are not suspected of self-sabotage; they become (almost) incalculable and priceless, requiring amends. In the British Journal of Sociology annual address, Nina Bandelj presents us with a kind of Ophelia, taking her point of departure from the death of childhood and the passage to its afterlife. These investments are part of the social life of childhood, and they involve a proliferation of monies. These monetary investments, Nigel Dodd reminds us, “are shaped by a range of historical, cultural, political, and institutional factors. They are complex and dynamic, variable and contested” (Dodd, 2016, p. 9). Bandelj demonstrates that in the US there has been a sharp increase in “parental investments” in children that differ from prior years in which there were simply “childrearing expenditures.” There are now tax instruments such as 529s and investment accounts large enough to purchase a home that are distinct from the monies set aside of schooling such as books, childcare, clothing, toys, birthday gifts, graduation presents, and the like. Like the shift from the useful to the priceless child, Bandelj marks the move from child-oriented spending for current times to child-based investments in the future. That future indicates the end of childhood and entry into adulthood–a new beginning. The question for parents and those monitoring them is whether the right investments were made to ensure safe passage to the next stage (Wherry, 2016, 2017). I will begin my commentary with the role of relational accounting in decisions to invest in children's education and will turn to how race works in investment choice. To make race active in interaction is to take into account how racialized histories shape investment priorities as well as the very menu of choices most available in and salient to different communities. I will conclude with a theoretical gem that is a bit buried in the discussion, that of economic entanglements. This final insight helps us better understand how different media of exchange affect other media by virtue of their proximity to one another. What is not fully accounted for in Bandelj's address is the fact that parents were not just investing more in children's education (in terms of dollars), but the cost of education has increased by about 400% over the last 30 years. If this were a home purchase, alarm bells would have sounded, and concerns would have been raised about how risky the investment might be. How could the same house go from $100,000 to $5- or $600,000 in price and cost more to finance? Is the interest rate reasonable or usurious? Is the home, or the educational institution, in the “right” neighborhood? The fact that there was not widespread concern or an insistence on the careful evaluation of this market means that individuals were not evaluating the risks of their investment in the same way as they could have. What were they doing instead? Sensitivity to the price of educational investments has declined as the life-stage significance of the investment has increased (Hayes & O’Brien, 2021; Wherry, 2016, 2017). The normal life-stages include birth, early childhood, the transition into young adulthood, and death. College represents the break between a non-adult and a young adult whose financial obligations are still associated with their families. Whereas parents feel obligated to pay for college expenses, including living expenses, they may not feel obligated to pay for a young adult who is not going to college, except in the case of emergencies. This happens, in part, due to shared expectations about the opportunities that a child should have in the transition to adulthood. Bandelj, Wherry, and Zelizer (2017, p. 7) observe that people are more reluctant to spend money saved for a child’s education because ‘these funds represent and reinforce meaningful family ties– the earmarking is relational’ (see also Zaloom, 2019) … investment monies by definition are uniquely oriented to the future… Wherry (2016, 134–135) advances a theory of relational accounting that accommodates the microlevel relational work involved both with specific earmarks and with collectively held codes that correspond to ritually marked moments or rites of passage. Financial goals such as retirement and college savings are thus morally fixed and structured. Graduations are costly, for example, and the expenses associated with the ceremony are not necessary for the acquisition of the credential or the human capital the graduating student now carries. Family members and neighbors, however, would object to a parent not supporting their child's participation in graduation and might themselves step in to help ensure that child experiences this meaningful right of passage. What is true for graduation is true for other investments in childhood. In a 3 year, longitudinal study of unconditional cash transfers, researchers found that “investments in child-specific goods [books, toys, and programs] and time spent with the child [reading to the child] …increased.” These findings contradict the notion that money is fungible, that these dollars are being used as any dollars coming into the family's coffers would be. Furthermore, their research design allows them to account for “the structure, format or related implementation features” of the cash transfer program. They write, “Notably, these investments occurred during the economically important first few years of children's development” (Gennetian et al., 2024, pp. 7–8). Yet, what they describe as a psychological, non-financial phenomenon, economic sociologists understand as relational accounting (Wherry, 2016, 2017). Relational accounting does not occur in a historical vacuum. How racial identities have formed in a country and how they have been shaped by public policy and by private market privations affect how families interpret and respond to investment opportunities. The racialized history of the United States has transformed some educational opportunities into debt traps. Six years after starting college, for example, a majority of Black students have not graduated but still carry student debts (Addo et al., 2016; Dwyer et al., 2012). With the educational investments being so risky for Black families, why do they pursue those high-risk investments, anyway? For too long, analysts pointed to information asymmetries and a problem with borrowers simply not understanding the stakes, along with students not “knowing the ropes” (how to navigate the college experience successfully). Bandelj turns the spotlight away from information gaps to the very relationships driving and sustaining those investment decisions. Tressie McMillan Cottom (2017) brings our racialized history back into our understanding of debt as it is expressed in the social gospel of education. Investing in one's education is participating in racial uplift. She studies for-profit colleges that train hairdressers, NASCAR technicians, medical and legal office administrators, and nurses along with nurses' aides. These are not the 4-year college experiences that come to mind in so many debates about what college is and who should go. And these college attendees believe strongly that they are investing in themselves. Their college debts, therefore, are positively associated, at least in the early years of having it, with their sense of mastery and self-esteem (Dwyer et al., 2011). There is a social gospel of progress that centers higher education as one of the rites of passage into adulthood (Wherry, 2016, 2017), and compliance to the gospel is socially enforced. While Bandelj's address emphasizes the vast differences in wealth by race that are driving how debts are accumulated for higher education, she does not detail how these material conditions are mobilized through relational work. She uses illustrative interview data from an upper middle-class white father of three to indicate the strong belief in investing in one's children, where “a loan is not the worst thing in the world,” and where it is “heartbreaking” to “want something for your kids that you cannot afford to get.” One has to wonder what the class and race differences are. Would a Black father say the same with a similar level of intensity? And what would happen if, by their actions, they violated their commitment to doing whatever possible to invest in their child's future? Would in-laws, siblings, grandparents, and other community members have a way of sanctioning those actions? How might racialized understandings modify risk tolerance and what effect might they have on investment portfolios? To treat “race as a structure as well as a structuring conditions” as scholars like Bonilla-Silva (2019), Feagin (2013), and Rucks-Ahidiana (2022) have done, is to make dynamic and processual its workings. In this process, the perceptions about and the salience of risk will vary, and that variation will be accomplished through interactional work (Wherry, 2012). Commercial engagements are performances, requiring the partial suspension of disbelief so that risks can be endured and the reactions of others interpreted. If we treat race as a structuring condition of performances, we must ask what individuals “see” right away versus how they exercise strategic ignorance towards facts whose acknowledgment would derail the performance. In other words, when negotiating which media of exchange are appropriate and which ones too risky to put into play, we are also responding to our histories of race and racialization that make some facts more salient than others. These histories of racialization shape how students invest in themselves and how their loved ones also contribute to those investments. Those histories also shape patterns of disinvestment, whereby opportunities that appeared to be capital appreciating turned into asset stripping traps (Wherry & Chakrabarti, 2022). More attention to how investments get racialized would result in an analysis of predatory inclusion (Taylor, 2019) in the higher education marketplace. Whether predatory or generative, monies for education are entangled. By their nature, monies wrap around one another the way tendrils do up the stalks of garden vegetables. Monies reach into the earth and become tied into other root systems. Pulling out a single strand is difficult without harming the very thing that the extrication might protect. How do our monied gardens grow, and under what conditions will they grow to seed? Bandelj begins to address this question with fresh theorizing about what economic entanglement means. She takes inspiration from quantum physics where quantum entanglement means that “aspects of one particle of an entangled pair depend on aspects of the other particle.” Bandelj clarifies further that “entanglement ‘exposes economic actors as practical negotiators employing procedural varieties of action, including commitment, muddling through, and improvisation’” (Bandelj, 2020, p. 255). I would suggest that the concept of entanglements does much more than expose the engagements of practical negotiators; it emplots them—placing monies and their users within a story-line that is being enacted (Alexander, 2004, 2011). To emplot actors engaged in relational work is also to consider the preferred versus the forbidden placements of the media they carry (Alexander, 2004). The exchange media themselves affect one another by virtue of their proximity to one another, their symbolic alignments or their binary oppositions. Some media, by nature or by law, might be repellant in proximity; others neutral or attractive, even before the users of the media take any actions to acknowledge, amplify, repair, cool, or cut a social tie. This means that relational packages are not just toolkits from which actors grab media of exchange (Swidler, 1986); the packages themselves do work once assembled and depending on the historical and the racialized contexts, some packages will resist the inclusion of particular forms of media, or of particular types of participants. The practice of emplotment puts monies into an ongoing narrative—be they assets or liabilities— in ways that prevent ontological rigidities (Somers, 1994). The assets and their ability to act, the liabilities and their power to impose penalties on other assets by way of levies, liens, garnishments, or even shame— they implicate the story of money for children with other stories about the kinds of futures these children deserve. Emplotted entanglements, I argue, might help us understand our “strange investments” in children's education (Dodd, 2011). In the investments parents make for their children, they are cultivating a kind of garden. Some gardens appear deserving of attention and applause, but others appear neglected and deserving only of what they got—the weeds. When too many weeds are permitted to possess the garden, they choke the good growth, leaving more space for the flourishing of bad investments. In time, these weeds can pull down the stronger, more mature trees rimming the original plot. The metaphor of the garden offers a warning even to those in class positions that seem to benefit from the current state of affairs. The conditions of one side can pollute the other. The separation between those in predatory versus non-predatory financial instruments can erode, even if those on the edges of predation do not believe themselves to be in imminent danger. In Bandelj's analysis of the plot, she witnesses childhood investments that have sprouted invasively across a field. There are not just a few but many ways to save and invest; not just a few, but many ways to borrow. As the plot grows wild, she captures the changing value of children and the changing investments made on their behalf. If we learn the lessons Bandelj is trying to teach us, we will revisit our investments, not just those made for children, and we will emplot them in the relational and racialized dramas shaping their salience.
