records.title: Editorial: Evidences (states and experiences) of land management and food/nutrition (in)security in mixed farming systems: a global perspective
records.authors: Tibebu Kassawmar; Gizaw Desta; Matebu Tadesse
records.abstract: The world is not on track to meet sustainable development goals for ending hunger, food insecurity, and malnutrition by 2030, with billions still lacking access to nutritious, safe, and sufficient food (Assefa et al., 2017;Iversen et al., 2023). The need to increase agricultural productivity in response to growing population has become a global concern (Wirsenius et al., 2010). As the world faces rapid population growth, climate change, and evolving market dynamics, rainfed farming systems are under increasing pressure to meet the growing demand for food and nutrition while also addressing the urgent need for environmental sustainability (Tully & Ryals, 2017). The challenge is not only to expand cultivated land and enhance agricultural productivity but also to manage land resources in ways that promote long-term ecological health, food security, and resilience to external shocks (Wani et al., 2009). One major sustainability issue is the limited agricultural space, which has become a critical concern as it is increasingly difficult to accommodate the growing of rainfed dependent rural population (Midmore, 2010). Expanding the arable landscape has been a vital strategy, but studies show that horizontal land expansion alone will not sustainably guarantee food security (Pretty, 1999). Ontop of limited agricultural space, mismanagement and progressive degradation of cultivated landscapes have worsened food insecurity, especially for smallholder farmers in developing countries (Zerssa et al., 2021). While conventional ways of Eenhancing grain productivity requires context-specific, innovative land use and management systems, yet effective solutions remain unclear (Wani et al., 2009). Recent recommendations underline that financing for food security and nutrition, along with effective tracking and innovative financing methods, is crucial for increasing investments needed to eradicate hunger and malnutrition (Iversen et al., 2023;Raj et al., 2022). The objective of the research topic were; (1) to explore innovative land use and management solutions to improve rural livelihoods and boost grain production, (2) to document the failures and success stories of land management strategies practiced across diverse regions of the world and finally (3) by highlighting the prevailing challenges in applying effective land use and livelihood systems, like the scalability issue, and indicating the need to co-designing of context and tailored land management solutions and (4) to identify and asses opportunities and challenges of addressing food security issues, Aiming to understand the challenges and opportunities of sustainable land management on food security, this editorial strive to compile about 23 researches with varied in content, themes and problem addressed. This editorial systematically synthesizes key findings from twenty-four research articles published on 'Land Management and Food/Nutrition (In)Security in Mixed Farming Systems' research topic. The key issues and findings from these articles are grouped into four sub-themes: namely; spatiotemporal dynamics of crop production, sustainable land and green water management, agricultural land management, productivity and Livelihood, and land tenure, gender and governance issues and their implications on food security. This editorial systematically synthesizes key findings of research articles published on 'Land Management and Food/Nutrition (In)Security in Mixed Farming Systems' research topic and presents as follows. Sustainable global food systems face multiple challenges, grain production declines in various parts of the world both size and productivity, although there is slight cropland area expansion in some regions. In many rainfed-dependent areas, the gap between cropland availability and grain demand remains large (Kassawmar et al., 2024a). Studies from Ethiopia and China show there is still considerable potential to increase grain production in rainfed regions of the world. Studies from Ethiopia and China indicate rainfed regions supporting landscapes of the worldwide hasve significant potential to boost grain production. In Ethiopia, about 60% of land is rainfed, providing an opportunity to address food insecurity and landlessness, but only 33% is cultivated due to biophysical, socio-economic, and institutional challenges (Kassawmar et al., a 2024a).On the other hand, a study in Ethiopia's Upper Blue Nile Basin found that cropland has increased by 10% since 1985, a small change compared to the population doubling every two decades A study findings from Ethiopia that assessed the spatiotemporal dynamics of grain producing landscapes of Ethiopia's Upper Blue Nile Basin revealed that, since 1985 cropland has increased by 10%, which is trivial compared to the doubling population every two decades (Kassawmar, et al., 2024b). The impacts of cropland expansion is minimal compared to grain volume gained through efficient cropping systems like residual farming, although got little attention by the government. However, the impact of increased grain production from efficient cropping systems like residual farming is greater than that of cropland expansion, despite receiving little attention from the government. A study in Northern China analyzed cropland changes over 40 years, revealing about 52 thousand km² expansion in grain-producing areas, primarily on black cotton soils, despite significant cropland loss from urban expansion, although A, study from northeast China highlights that utilizing black cotton soils expanded grain production areas but struggles with land aggregation and biodiversity loss. (He, et al.m 2024). Such scientific evidences offer opportunities to invent appropriate land management systems. TheyThis underpins the importance of policy support for land and water management strategies, especially expansion of croplands in low-elevation areas and multiple cropping systems in black cotton soils and floodplains. Another similar study in Northern China, examined the spatiotemporal dynamics of croplands over the last 40 years and found that grain-producing landscapes expanded by 51,976.76 km², mostly on black cotton soils (He, et al., 2024), although a considerable area of croplands has been lost due to urban expansion. Such scientific evidences offer opportunities to invent appropriate land management systems and develop policy strategies for sustainable food systems.Research findings compiled from 134 developing countries showed that sustainable intensification requires a combination of strategies tailored to local contexts and environmental conditions, rather than a single practice (Mabhaudhi et al., 2024). In rainfed and mixed farming systems, diversified grain production strategies are essential as they have great potential to copy climate change risks while enhancing multiple ecosystem services. In Ethiopia, intensifying rainfed farming systems through multiple cropping systems can better address landlessness and food security than technological and capital intensive options like irrigation (Kassawmar et al., 2024a). Combining intensification strategies like multiple cropping and mixed farming, along with land management practices such as land restoration and utilizing marginal landscapes, can boost agricultural productivity and ecosystem services. However, this requires investment in extension services and farming technologies.Given the challenges of efficiency, productivity, and political or technological barriers to expanding cropland, the focus should be on implementing multiple-harvest strategies on existing cultivated lands (Kassawmar et al., 2024a). A, study from northeast China highlights that utilizing black cotton soils expanded grain production areas but struggles with land aggregation and biodiversity loss. A study in northwestern Ethiopia found that since the 1990s, smallholder farmers expanded eucalyptus plantations into croplands, but reverse the trend by 2017/18 due to market changes (Zeleke et al., 2024). An interesting lesson found from this study was, surprisingly, clearing eucalyptus plantations led to higher yields than continuously ploughed cereal fields, challenging the belief that eucalyptus harms productivity (Daba, 2016). The study found that converting cropland to eucalyptus led to significant grain losses at various scales, while also raising unexpected and controversial land tenure issues. This indicates that smallholders often prioritize short-term economic factors over long-term ecological and social concerns, highlighting the need for adaptive, context-specific land management strategies (Zeleke et al., 2024).Managing land and water, key natural capitals in agriculture, is a critical global research focus. A major challenge in sustainable food systems is balancing land use for competing needs like food, feed, timber, and energy. This has led researchers to explore effective strategies for managing agricultural land and green water (Kassawmar et al., 2024a). According to Kassawmar et al., 2024a, Uunlocking the potential of Ethiopia's rainfed landscapes could enhance food security and support millions more people (Kassawmar et al., 2024a). A study on land use strategies in Ethiopia's rRainfed cCropping aArea found that 60% of the country is rainfed, offering significant potential to combat food insecurity and landlessness. The study emphasizes the need for a holistic approach to agricultural development, acknowledging the links between land, water, and food security. While 33% of this area is used for grain production, supporting 120 million people, the remaining 67% of uncultivated land could benefit millions more smallholders (Kassawmar et al., 2024a). The study revealed that 16% of the uncultivated land is suitable for crop production, but requires technological investments and addressing political challenges. The study emphasizes the need for a holistic approach to agricultural development, acknowledging the links between land, water, and food security.Another study in Eastern Cape, South Africa, found that inadequate adaptation strategies by smallholder farmers resulted in poor land use performance, limiting resource optimization for food security. (Tantoh and McKay, 2024). Another A study from Ethiopian study highlights the potential for expanding cropland through efficient systems like residual farming. However, it suggests that producing more grain is more achievable through efficient multiple cropping practices than by simply expanding agricultural land. Smallholders can benefit more by utilizing marginal areas through soil and water conservation measures and adopting multiple cropping systems such as residual moisture farming, flood farming, short rainy season farming, agroforestry, and mixed cropping. (Kassawmar et al., 2024b andDesta et al., 2024a). Non-crop farming systems, such as livestock farming and eco-tourism, are also have untapped potentials to ensure resilient livelihood systems. A study from Benin, West Africa, found that agroforestry, combining trees with livestock, is an effective strategy for optimizing land and green water (Assani et al., 20243).Effective land and water use can be achieved through evidence-based planning aligned with food security and environmental goals. A study in China's Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region shows that a balanced land allocation strategy, emphasizing crop diversity for better nutrition, reduces land fragmentation and enhances food security (Wang et al., 2024). Another study from Ethiopia show that integrated, data-driven approaches-through agroforestry, resource management, and technology-can strengthen smallholder farming systems landscape segmented flood risk management and flood farming techniques agroforestry, resource management, and technology-can strengthen smallholder farming systems under drought conditions (Desta et al., 2024b). These research findings emphasize the importance of smart agriculture and land use planning in optimizing inputs like fertilizers, pesticides, and water, boost productivity while ensuring environmental sustainability. Sustainable agriculture requires balancing economic, social, and environmental goals, focusing on local contexts, and empowering farmers to integrate adaptive farming with food and environmental objectives. This requires huge investment on innovations and strengthening spatial technology applications.In the pursuit of resilient livelihoods and sustainable farming, studies in India, Ethiopia, China, and Pakistan have highlighted the importance of innovative farming practices. Effective land management, including soil health management, conservation practices, and agroforestry, can enhance soil health and productivity, contributing to sustainable livelihoods. In Pakistan, using biochar, organic fertilizers, and targeted soil amendments on upland rice helped to narrow down yield gaps and boosting production on nutrient-deficient soils (Santosa et al., 2024). A study from Ethiopia shows that, compared to conventional farms, soil and water conservation practices have greatly improved soil quality in degraded landscapes (Tebeje et al., 2024). However, the overall benefits remain limited, mainly due to lack of integration with other technologies. To ensure longterm benefits of soil and water managements, rainfed based mixed farming needs context-specific strategies. In smallholder mixed farming systems, farmers often face losses from blanket applications of costly fertilizers, as they cannot match fertilizer use with crop nutrient needs. Challenges such as extreme soil variability, lack of spatial evidences, and inadequate knowledge and poor government support hinder effective nutrient management. A study from Ethiopia showed that applying landscape-specific fertilizer at different slope positions significantly increased yield, offering higher profits than traditional blanket applications (Desta, et al., 20234). Such and similar approaches help reduce yield gaps and improve nutrient use efficiency, with potential for scaling through further innovations. In contrast, studies from Northeast China highlight the negative impacts of cropland aggregation on soil health, emphasizing the need for better management. A study from India's Jammu region stressed that agroforestry systems provide valuable ecosystem services and enhance rural incomes compared to other cropping systems (Kumar et al., 2024). Despite its benefits, agroforestry is underused due to limited awareness and support, with key technical challenges in optimizing crop-tree spatial arrangements and balancing tree canopies with crops.While land management efforts focus on boosting grain production and resilient food systems, non-farm activities, limited attention and advocacy given to them is very limited while they are crucial for resilient livelihoods (Baghernejad, et al., 2024). Land management approaches, such as integrated farming in Benin and land use optimization in China, show that smallholder mixed farming prioritizes productivity resilience over food security and livelihood resilience. Scholars stress that, to effectively enhance livelihood resilience, exploring non-agricultural income diversification and integrating with agricultural sustainability is critical. Given smallholder based agriculture sector has limited employment opportunities, non-farm livelihoods should be considered although a successful livelihood stabilization is not trivial. As there is a risk of shifting entirely from agriculture to non-farm activities like tourism, a study from Benin highlights the need for careful integration of agricultural with non-agricultural systems and prevent sudden decline of grain production.The application of advanced technologies like mobile apps and remote sensing have become crucial to promote effective land management practices and improve land productivity. In Ethiopia, a mobile app providing landscape-specific fertilizer recommendations helps optimize input use, increase yields, and enhance farmer profitability (Desta, et al., 2024). Another study from China demonstrated that following China's digital transformation and agricultural modernization, digital technologies have become vital in facilitating agricultural supply and boosting sustainable land use (Liang,, et al., 2024). Although both land transfer and iInternet use promote crop rotation, the former has stronger effect in specifically benefiting older farmers, the latter benefits more the younger ones. Promoting crop rotation through stable land rights and incentivized land transfer can boost sustainable livelihoods and productivity.Global studies emphasize the role of land governance, tenure systems, and gender in improving agricultural productivity. Adaptive land management is crucial for sustainable development, especially in influencing farmers' behaviors. A case study from China evaluated farmers' perception on the resilience of the cultivated land use system (Wang and Wang, 2024) and found that farmers' cultivated land use systems exhibit uneven resilience, generally labeled as low production resilience. Poor production efficiency and limited ecological protection indicate weak functioning of the cultivated land use system. Thus highlights strategic needs to improve production resilience, encourage investment in land resources, promote ecological protection, and enhance willingness for land transfer.The separating three rights policy in China's land system reform, has positively impacted rural livelihoods and incomes although the effects vary across farmers group (Hu, et al., 2024). Since the inception of the reform, farmers who got more training, have larger croplands, and those growing food crops benefit the most by the policy. Although further research is needed to fully understand the direct impacts of the policy, the findings unveiled directly linkage of income with investment, credit access, and non-agricultural employment opportunities. A study using provincial data from China found that farmland transfer and agricultural loans positively correlate with grain production, though agricultural loans have a negative effect (Ding, et al., 2024). This suggests that financial activities access enhance farmland efficiency and grain production, emphasizing the need for government support in land reforms and agricultural finance.Another study in South Africa, where there is critical gender related land issues, rural women's have limited access to land, hindering their economic opportunities (Masuku et al., 2024). Gender disparities in land access remain a significant challenge in rural South Africa, as customary law challenges women in acquiring equal land ownership. Land reform for equal access is essential for reducing food insecurity and promoting gender equality in agriculture (Ding, et al., 2024). Evidences from a case study in China, support the importance of land transfer, which promotes crop rotation and improved land use, while addressing land ownership issues. These findings urge developing countries like South Africa to create land policies that address gender disparities in land access and ownership, as they negatively affect food security. Lessons learned during COVID-19 pandemic highlights that the disruption of global food supply chains during global shocks can only be addressed by building food supply systems proactively (Tian, and Mei, 2024). A study from Chad showed that while food insecurity had been rising before the pandemic, food security improved after the shock, indicating the impact of increased awareness and knowledge gained from the pandemic's effects ( Kang, et al, 2024).In summary, an important concluding remark from the synthesized scientific evidences is that appropriate land use systems and efficient agricultural water management strategies alone cannot enhance incomes and ensure sustainable food system. Rather access to land, markets, financial resources, and extension services are also essential, especially empowering women, are key to sustainability. BesidesBesides, to promoting regenerative agriculture and multiple cropping systems authors underline the importance of promoting non-farm activities as they can play crucial role in stabilizing livelihoods and boosting resilience of food systems. Technologies like remote sensing, GIS, and mobile apps tools can leverage precision farming, and further enhance crop yields and environmental sustainability. Promoting agricultural technology and digital literacy, specifically rural digitalization, help young farmers adopt sustainable practices and further improve productivity and safeguard food supply chains.We hope this Research Topic of articles on emerging agricultural practices and ways to sustain food production will be useful to scientists, agricultural educators, government regulators, and other relevant stakeholders of food production. We also hope that they will serve as a good course on a global scale to help mitigate improper land use and management, especially on crop production. Authors believed that these published articles are going to impact to a wide range of readers with an insight into practical sustainable agricultural land and water management and technologies among the smallholder farming systems. Authors recommended more in-depth, systematic assessment that spans local, continental, and global scales is crucial because:1. Local Scale: The conditions and challenges at the local level often differ significantly, so it's essential to tailor strategies to local needs. For example, water availability, soil fertility, and access to energy resources vary from region to region and need to be considered in food systems. 2. Continental Scale: At the continental level, broader patterns such as climate variability, population growth, and economic trends come into play. Continental policies and infrastructure can also impact resource use and distribution, and solutions need to consider trade, policy coordination, and regional cooperation. 3. Global Scale: Global factors such as climate change, international trade agreements, and global supply chains influence resource availability and food security across regions. Policies that consider these interconnected global challenges can help in fostering a more equitable and sustainable food system.By looking at the land-water-food-energy nexus across these scales, can identify and solutions that the demand for food, water, and the health of requires efforts combining and as as data and to ensure long-term sustainability.

Mark Rank and Thomas Hirschl have done a related calculation, also using PSID data. They ask what share of Americans experience five or more total years of income below the poverty line, of welfare receipt, or of unemployment between the ages of 25 and 60. The answer is 35 percent. See Rank and Hirschl, forthcoming. See also Dynan, Elmendorf, and Sichel 2012. Elizabeth Jacobs, personal communication. Families USA 2009. Mendes 2012, using Gallup data. Jacoby 2012. Pew Research Center. For more, see Page and Jacobs 2009; McCall 2013. Sen 1999; Nussbaum 2011. Noah 2012. The share of women aged 25 to 29 who have completed four or more years of college has risen steadily over the past half century. In fact, by the early 1990s women had caught up with men in college graduation, and in the ensuing decades they raced ahead. By 2010, 36 percent of women aged 25 to 29 had completed college, compared to just 28 percent of men. This gap in favor of women was as large as the gap favoring men was in 1960. (Census Bureau, “Educational Attainment: CPS Historical Time Series Tables,” table A-2, using Current Population Survey data.) Women have made significant strides in employment as well. According to OECD data, in 1960 just 41 percent of prime-working-age (25 to 54) women were employed. By 2010 that had jumped to 73 percent. Among men in this age group, the employment rate fell from 92 percent to 87 percent. Median earnings among women employed full-time and year round likewise have risen steadily, from (in 2010 dollars) $21,000 in 1960 to $28,000 in 1979 to $38,000 in 2010 (Census Bureau, “Historical Income Tables,” table P-21.). This is an advance in an absolute sense and also relative to men. In the 1960s and 1970s, women’s median earnings were about 60 percent of men’s. In the 1980s women began gaining ground, and by 2010 the ratio was 77 percent. In fact, if we narrow the comparison to those aged 25 to 34, the ratio is 91 percent. (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2011. The female-to-male earnings ratio then decreases for older age groups, partly because women are much more likely to leave work temporarily for family reasons. Part of the gap is accounted for by work hours (men are more likely to work overtime) and employee benefits (women are more likely to hold jobs with better benefits but lower pay). See CONSAD Research Corp 2009.) As of 2012 women held 52 percent of managerial, professional, and related positions (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2011). At the top of the corporate hierarchy there is still a large gender gap; yet here, too, progress has been significant. Women represent only 18 percent of senior officers (vice president or higher) in Fortune 500 firms, but that’s up from 9 percent in 1995. Women hold only 3 percent of Fortune 500 CEO slots, yet that’s up from 1 percent in 2000. At the very top, on the boards of directors of Fortune 500 companies, women hold 16 percent of the seats, up from 1 percent in 1988. (These data are from Catalyst, catalyst.org.) All told, women’s capabilities have expanded markedly. Noteworthy gaps with men persist in various aspects of labor market success, but progress has been substantial. In 1960, only 40 percent of African Americans aged 25 to 29 had completed high school. By the end of the 1970s, the share had increased to 77 percent, and in 2010 it reached 89 percent (this includes those with a GED). The advance was not only absolute, but also relative to whites. records.abstract: GAAP have permitted private sector and public sector organizations to present particular gains and losses as extraordinary items on the operating statement if certain criteria are met. The application of the criteria has evolved over time resulting in different treatment for similar events in the private sector compared to the public sector. This paper traces the evolution of extraordinary items and examines examples of these differing treatments.Beginning with the 2008 tax year, the Internal Revenue Service has dramatically increased the reporting requirements in the Form 990 information return for tax-exempt organizations. Non-profit organizations are now required to go well beyond the traditional reporting of revenues and costs. The new “core” return has eleven pages that must be supplemented with up to sixteen schedules. Non-profit organizations will now have to present detailed lists of board members and key employees along with explanations of their policies on record-keeping and the destruction of documents, executive compensation, conflicts of interest, affiliations with both exempt and taxable organizations, including those outside of the U.S., as well as very specific accountings of fundraising activities, the management of donated property, and the use of bond proceeds. While the return makes clear that all of these policies are not required to maintain tax-exempt status, simply answering “no policy in place” may well cast the organization in an unfavorable light to the IRS, potential donors and board members, the media and others. The new Form 990 confronts virtually every tax-exempt organization with an imposing array of policy creation and revision.SAP (ERP) software requires significant effort to use on a daily basis as well as introducing the software in a classroom setting. ERP system software is exceedingly costly, complex, and difficult to comprehend which makes it difficult to work with. This has discouraged many companies and faculty members from becoming more knowledgeable regarding the software's capabilities. However, the market is changing rapidly regarding the sale and implementation of ERP systems in organizations throughout the USA. For the last decade, the Fortune 1,000 companies have used ERP systems, but smaller companies have not. As the competition has heated up in ERP system software in the last few years, the cost of this software has dropped significantly and has become easier to implement and use. This has resulted in a significant number of mid and smaller companies to implement the ERP software. Many more students will be confronted with an ERP system when they get their first job. The model introduced here seeks to illustrate that there are some basic objectives that need to be understood by managerial accounting students. This can be accomplished in an efficient, less time consuming way than previously possible.With the development and widespread use of internet technology, businesses have changed the way they operate by using the internet as a marketing tool to expand their businesses and reach new potential customers. Online marketing has evolved in the past twelve years as a marketing medium that has the most potential to increase awareness for a company and launch it into the worldwide market. As a result, businesses are faced with a new challenge: How to create a successful online marketing campaign. This paper will focus on the history and current development, as well as, future trends of online marketing, in order to explore both past and evolving internet marketing techniques. With new ideas and new web technology being developed every day, online marketing has not yet reached its full potential and in the future, marketing experts project that most companies will move primarily to online strategies in order to reach increasing numbers of customers. It is therefore essential that companies develop the most effective strategies for using this important medium.During economic downturns, companies look to reduce employee costs and employees search for ways to earn additional income. One way to reduce labor costs is to convert employees to independent contractor status. To earn additional income, individuals can start a new business. Many businesses and individuals are considering these options today, so the purpose of this paper is to highlight the numerous tax implications both situations present. Specifically, the factors the IRS and courts consider when classifying a worker as either an employee or an independent contractor are examined, as well as, the tax implications an individual faces under each status. For individuals seeking to start a new business, the factors the IRS and courts look to when classifying a start-up activity as either a business or a hobby are discussed. This determination ultimately dictates whether all ordinary and necessary expenses of the activity will be deductible in full or severely limited. Lastly, because the decision of how to operate a new business influences both the business and tax objectives an owner can achieve, the tax implications of entity choice (e.g., sole proprietor, regular corporation, S corporation, or LLC) are also analyzed.In November of 2001, at the age of 55, I became one of the earlier members of our baby boomer cadre in academia to experience and survive a stroke. At that time, my entire left side was paralyzed. After rehabilitation therapy I was able to regain the ability to walk, but unfortunately I have not yet been able to regain significant usable functioning of my left arm and hand. This is quite a “nuisance”, given that I had been left-handed before the stroke. This factor makes it rather tedious and frustrating to operate a computer keyboard, for example. The purpose of this paper is to report some of the technological adaptions that I have assimilated and adopted since the time of the stroke, including the use of Dragon Naturally Speaking and a Segway, which have allowed me to continue functioning effectively as a full-time professor, despite my physical limitations.Capital asset pricing model and Fama-French model are popular with accounting and finance professionals due to their unambiguous description of the factors used in their models. records.title: Basic Capital:
records.abstract: It is not often that radical ideas entertained by egalitarian political theorists and philosophers have an immediate impact on public policy. This paper looks at how one such proposal, the idea of a universal capital grant or “basic capital,” did apparently impact public policy in the UK in the form of the Child Trust Fund (CTF) enacted under the previous, Labour government. Some supporters of the CTF (such as the author) viewed it as potentially an important first-step towards the creation of something like a “property-owning democracy.”1The victory, however, was mixed and looks to have been short-lived. The new Coalition government abolished the CTF in 2010 as part of its austerity program. In light of this, the paper considers the future prospects for basic capital. Can philosophy once again connect with real politics? If so, how?Let's begin by clarifying what basic capital is and why it seems to be an important contribution to the institutional framework of a just society.Many readers will be familiar with the idea of unconditional basic income. Every citizen receives a periodic, cash income grant from the state which is unconditional with respect to means (income and wealth from other sources) and employment history or willingness to take employment. Basic capital (BC hereafter) is similar except that the grant takes the form of a one-off lump-sum payment to the citizen rather than a periodic income grant. Typically, the proposal is to endow citizens with BC early in their adult years. Sometimes proponents of BC argue that the grant should not be available simply as cash but that it should be limited to a range of uses. The menu of options might include: paying for higher education or vocational training, putting down a deposit on a house, or setting up a new business. While a few see the policy as an alternative to more familiar welfare state arrangements, others view the idea more as a complement to income transfers and public services.The proposal is usually traced back at least as far as Tom Paine's Agrarian Justice of 1797, in which Paine proposed: “… A PLAN FOR MELIORATING THE CONDITION OF MAN, BY CREATING IN EVERY NATION A NATIONAL FUND, To pay to every Person, when arrived at the Age of TWENTY-ONE YEARS, the Sum of FIFTEEN POUNDS Sterling, to enable HIM or HER to begin the World!”2Some two hundred years later, Paine's idea was taken up by Bruce Ackerman and Anne Alstott in their 1999 book, The Stakeholder Society.3 Ackerman and Alstott proposed that every US citizen should receive a grant of $80,000 on maturity. Receiving the full grant would be conditional on completing High School and not having a criminal record. Young adults would only get full control of the capital in their early twenties, but would be able to access it before then to help finance higher education. Ackerman and Alstott proposed that the BC be funded initially from a wealth tax. In the longer term, the policy would be financed out of a tax on the estates of those who had originally received the stakeholder grant. Thus, as with Paine, Ackerman and Alstott envisage a system of citizen's inheritance in which a portion of intergenerational wealth transfers is channelled through the state to establish a reasonable endowment of wealth for all in early adulthood.Ackerman and Alstott based their case for BC on two main ethical considerations: equality of opportunity and freedom.Let's start with the argument from equality of opportunity. The initial normative premise, of course, is that justice requires (amongst other things) some form of equality of opportunity. By this is meant not simply formal equality to compete for jobs and offices, but a more substantive equality that weakens the connection between chances for occupational attainment and parental social class.4 The degree to which society satisfies this conception of equal opportunity is affected—or so it is claimed—by a range of factors which includes inequality in access to financial assets (perhaps especially in early adulthood when key life-shaping decisions are made). If this is true, then a policy of BC can be expected to help reduce inequality in initial endowments of financial assets and thereby promote equality of opportunity.Turning to the argument from freedom, we can distinguish at least two lines of thought in Ackerman's and Alstott's work. The first appeals to what we can call freedom as independence. It appeals to a notion of freedom similar to that which republican philosophers, notably Philip Pettit, have termed freedom as ‘non-domination.’5 An individual has independence to the extent that she/he is able to live without being ‘at the mercy’ of more powerful others (employers, spouses, bureaucrats). Independence in this sense is compromised when one relies on another—employer, spouse, bureaucrat—for access to a basic income. Owning one's own assets enhances independence by giving one a source of income that others do not control. Ackerman and Alstott refer to this ideal of freedom as independence when they quote the British economist James Meade on the importance of property ownership: “A man with … property has … bargaining strength and a sense of security, independence, and freedom …. He can snap his fingers at those on whom he must rely for income, for he can always rely for a time on his capital.”6There is, however, another dimension of freedom in play in Ackerman's and Alstott's case for BC. Ackerman and Alstott comment that, in the absence of BC: “… just at the moment we expect young adults to make responsible life-shaping decisions, we do not afford them the resources they need to take a responsible long-term perspective ….”7 What comes into focus here, I think, is the individual's interest in what we may call opportunity for ambition formation. We all have an interest in being able, in our early adult years, to approach life with ambition (not necessarily in the narrow materialist or positional senses of the term). We have an interest in being able to meaningfully pose, and act on our considered answer to, the question: “What do I want to do with my life?” Being unable to pose this question meaningfully in our early adult years is arguably of particular concern because, as said, this is when many of us make key, life-shaping choices. This, I think, is what Tom Paine is alluding to in his evocative notion of “beginning the world.”8The empirical conjecture is that a lack of financial assets and related opportunities in early adult life can threaten opportunity for ambition formation. It might do so in two ways (both noted in Ackerman's and Alstott's discussion). First, there is what we may term the distraction effect. Lacking assets, the immediate imperative simply to make ends meet militates against seriously posing questions about one's life goals. Second, there is what we may call the horizons effect. Even if you have the time and energy to think about one's life goals, a lack of assets can seriously limit one's ability to ‘think big’ about them. One trims one's life goals to suit one's limited resources. If the empirical conjecture is correct, then the ownership of assets in early adulthood, by working against these two effects, can help secure adequate opportunity for ambition formation.9When Ackerman and Alstott published The Stakeholder Society in 1999, the political context in the UK was one which made for a favourable reception of their book. Earlier in the decade, ‘centre-left’ thinking in the UK had been strongly preoccupied by Will Hutton's arguments for “stakeholder capitalism,” as set out in his best-selling The State We're In.10 Hutton's stakeholder capitalism looked in particular to the German economy for inspiration. It implied new institutions to democratise the economy, bringing workers' representatives into the governance of firms and workplaces. It implied a different relationship between finance and industry to the one that, according to Hutton, had served British industry so poorly. However, as the so-called ‘New Labour’ project developed in the mid-1990s, a different understanding of “stakeholder capitalism” began to emerge. Critics argued that German institutions were not an appropriate model for the UK. The British centre-left should try to develop its own conception of “stakeholding” to suit its own, more ‘liberal’ form of capitalism. In the words of the economist, David Soskice: “Stakeholding Yes; the German Model No.”11 As Rajiv Prabhakar has noted, the result was a shift in the meaning of the “stakeholding” rhetoric.12 “Stakeholding” was not about relationships of reciprocity and mutual empowerment within the firm or enterprise, but about ensuring a wider dispersion of individual assets or “stakes” (of human and financial capital). Thus, the title of Ackerman's and Alstott's book advocating BC spoke directly to this reframed rhetoric of stakeholding within the Labour party—a party which had returned to government after a landslide election victory in 1997.Viewed in context, therefore, it is perhaps not at all surprising that the year following the publication of The Stakeholder Society, two leading UK think-tanks, both with strong links to the Labour party, published proposals for forms of BC. From the Fabian Society came David Nissan's and Julian Le Grand's A Capital Idea: Start-Up Grants for Young People.13 This argued for the introduction of a £10,000 capital grant for all citizens at age 18. This would be paid for by higher taxes of inherited wealth (they envisaged a total tax take of 25 percent of the total annual transfer of wealth across the generations). The grants would be available to use for a restricted range of purposes: higher education, vocational training, housing deposits, establishing a new business.From the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) came Gavin Kelly's and Rachel Lissauer's Ownership for All.14 This argued for a £1,000 grant for all children at birth to be invested in a Children's Opportunity Fund. This would accumulate as the child grew up. Families would be encouraged to save into the accounts. The state would match the savings of low-income families (e.g., £1 from the state into the account for every £1 saved by a low-income family). The money would be locked into the accounts until the child reached 18 when he or she would be able to use them for a restricted range of purposes (similar to those envisaged by Nissan and Le Grand).The proposals stimulated a debate within the Labour government on the merits and design of a policy along these lines. The eventual result was the Child Trust Fund, enacted in 2004 but backdated to include all children born after September 2002. Under this initiative: 1.Each child received a grant at birth which was placed in a personal investment account (their Child Trust Fund or CTF) to accumulate in value while they grew up.2.The initial grant was £250 for most children, £500 for those in low-income families (the poorest third). The government planned to make a top-up payment into the accounts, of similar amounts, at age seven.3.The child's family was free to contribute up to £1,200 to the account in a given year.4.Once invested, the funds were locked into the account until the child reached 18.5.On maturity (age of 18) the child would be free to access the account as he or she wished.In moving from the original Fabian Society and IPPR proposals to the actual policy of the CTF, the Labour government faced a number of key design issues.15 First: Should the policy be a pure capital grant or a capital grant boosted by a family saving component? The Ackerman and Alstott and Fabian Society proposals were for pure capital grants, whereas the IPPR proposal was for an initial state endowment to be topped up by family saving (with a program of matched savings to assist low-income households). The IPPR proposal reflected a second important academic influence, the work of the US social policy expert Michael Sherraden on “Individual Development Accounts” (IDAs). IDAs are saving accounts for low-income households, which work on the basis of matched contributions: for every dollar saved by the account-holder, a third party matches that with a dollar (or with more or less depending on the matching ratio). Sherraden argues that matched saving programs of this kind are an effective way to help poor people accumulate an asset and have positive effects on their sense of self and capacity.16A second design question was: Should the state put restrictions on how people may use their capital accounts at 18? Unlike the Ackerman and Alstott proposal, both the Fabian Society and IPPR proposals included restrictions on what young adults may use their capital grants for. The latter were clearly responding to a concern for what Ackerman and Alstott term “stakeblowing”: the worry that young people might simply ‘blow’ their capital grants on immediate consumption or imprudent investments.Third: Should the state link the capital grant to an inheritance tax? Ackerman and Alstott's and the Fabian Society's proposals included such a link, while the IPPR's did not.In the event, as we can see from the above description of the CTF, the government resolved the design questions in favour of there being: a large saving component to complement state endowments; no restrictions on use of the capital account at 18; and no link to inheritance tax. The CTF was presented as an example of “asset-based welfare.” Asset-based welfare would be a “fourth pillar” of the welfare state alongside income transfers, public services and labour market policy to promote high levels of employment.In at least two key respects, then, the CTF was very much a compromise on the ideal of Basic Capital (BC). There was no link to inheritance tax, and hence the policy did not fully reflect the vision of citizen's inheritance evident in Paine's, Ackerman's and Alstott's and the Fabian Society's proposals.But perhaps more significantly, the relative weighting given to the state endowment and family saving in the CTF meant that the amounts children could expect to hold on maturity would be highly dependent on their family's ability and willingness to save. Government calculations suggested that a child born into a poor family receiving the initial endowment from the state plus state top-up at age seven but no additional family contributions into the CTF would end up with about £2,000 at age 18. In stark contrast, a child born into a more affluent family which saved the annual maximum of £1,200 into the account could expect around £36,000 at 18.17For supporters of BC, therefore, the CTF was by no means a but very much the first-step in the of an effective BC. there was clearly a need to the of potentially very accounts at 18 to family One was to the state contribution towards low-income households). was for the state to assist saving into the funds by low-income households, by the idea in the original IPPR proposal for the state to match the savings of low-income into for such could perhaps from a inheritance tax (or some other form of wealth the time as this in the interest in BC and the CTF developed the CTF was in the UK initially by both Labour and the However, the the of the main in the of it from the the election on a to the CTF and use the public funds for other This was in many ways an for the party to The idea of BC is arguably a example of a social policy. records.title: Four Elegies
records.abstract: The Australian opals were beautiful, one had to concede that. Their blues had all the depth of lapis; the greens glinted with the brilliance of emeralds, like water transmuted into fire. Bessie Gruber could well imagine the love that caused her son and his new wife to part with their limited funds, thinking that there could be no better gift for a woman who so loved beauty. The difficulty was this: The stones would bring bad luck, as everyone knew, or ought to. Their iridescence was enchanting, but also uncanny, like a cat's eye, or the evil eye. Objects like these had power, though people nowadays might choose to ignore that fact. But to her way of thinking, matter was not just inert dust, and mind no abstract conceit. Each affected the other in ways that were not always easy to predict. These were forces a person didn't want to mess with. So down the toilet the opals went.The world she'd grown up in had been more congenial to her point of view. In the 1910s and 1920s descendants of German settlers living in southeastern Pennsylvania still practiced a type of faith healing called “powwowing,” a tradition that dated back to at least the eighteenth century. Powwowing was one part herbal lore, one part prayer, and one part harmless nonsense. Warts, for example, could be cured by planting the cut halves of a potato under the eaves in the light of a waxing moon. To manage aagewasche, or stomach cramp in infants, you simply measured the child with a bit of red string, and passed him around a table leg. More advanced practitioners claimed to be able to cast out demons, but an honest powwower gave modern medicine its due. Only a dumkopf would try to cure diphtheria with prayer alone.Homebound and shy, sensible and kind, with a mind that was sharp, yet capacious enough to allow for the possibility of forces existing beyond the realm of science, Bessie seemed a good candidate to carry on the old arts. An aunt on her father's side who powwowed offered to instruct her, but her mother vetoed the plan. Powwowing was backward nonsense, something only “the dumb Dutch” would believe. Even so, it could bring trouble: In 1929 a practitioner in the nearby town of York had been murdered by an acquaintance who believed he'd been hexed. Bessie was closer to her mother than anyone in the world, and Sarah Heiser Hartmann had never been a woman to brook disagreement.For a time, it seemed as though her fate would be bound by her mother's opinions and needs. At nineteen she had every reason to expect that what her girlfriends had would be hers as well. First, a season or two of fun (being crowned Queen of the May, trips to New York to see the latest fashions), which would then lead naturally to marriage and children. But when the Depression came her father's bakery failed, he hastened its decline by giving away bread to neighbors in need. Bessie, with her teacher's certificate and history degree, was the sole source of income for herself and her parents. It would be ten years before she'd meet her husband by chance at a college reunion. When he came to call, her mother was suspicious. “That man is looking for a woman,” she said. Bessie, twenty-nine by this time, decided there was nothing so very wrong with that.There was no white satin gown, no lace veil, no crown of flowers at the wedding of these two schoolteachers. As befitted lean times, the dress was simple and practical: navy blue rayon with an allover pattern, in white, of trellises and vines. The pattern was important, because plainness on such an occasion would have been an affront. Her ancestors painted hex signs on their barns to keep away evil spirits; she too believed that beauty was the ultimate hedge against malevolence. An empty corner was not just a place where dust gathered, but provided a toehold for evil. One had to keep those spaces filled, with pictures on easels or with fragile embroidered chairs, just as one had to tie red ribbons around the neck of every vase and cover the surfaces of breadboxes and hutches, headboards and seat backs with lovebirds and tulips and vines. This was not materialism, but a form of externalized prayer. By the time her grandchildren were born, her house had become a veritable wunderkammer, as intricate as a cloisonné brooch.How did they work, these continual spells against ruin? They could not prevent her husband from developing severe depression, which stalked him intermittently from his fifties until the end of his life. They could not prevent cancer, or bring back the finger amputated in her fifties to stop the spread of the disease. Nor could they halt, in the final decades of her life, the desecration of her beloved Pennsylvania countryside as asphalt and strip malls replaced the farms and country lanes she'd explored as a girl. These things mattered a great deal, but on the whole hers had been a good life, and a sweet one. Thinking made it so.As is true of so many of us, an outsider saw her best. Her son's wife scoffed at her superstitions, but in generous moments could concede that there was some quality in her mother-in-law's mien and bearing that called to mind a Romanian princess. The invocation of Romanian royalty specifically was curious, for at the time the country was locked away behind the Iron Curtain, and no one in the family had ever been there, or had any roots in that place. But Romania's actuality, its existence on a map or in the world, was not what mattered. Romania in this context was a symbol, a stand-in for all that was magical and unknowable, the opposite of ordinary. Romania was the enchanted castle, the crystal inside the geode, the witch's hut in the middle of the forest where you might find succor—provided you were pure of heart.Perhaps she found a use for such a place during her final battle with metastatic melanoma. There was no magic that could help her at that point, no healing charm to beat back the renegade cells. But then, cheating death had never been the point. The best faith healers believed that natural and the supernatural were not completely separate realms, but streams that ran parallel to each other and met up once in a while, at points. Magic, so called, was only the trick of catching those points of convergence and riding them, just as a trout might emerge from a still pool and join the swifter current, or a hawk might catch an updraft and rise into the air.And at the end of a long life, those streams converged anyway. People somehow became their own archetypes. To her granddaughters she'd always resembled a sorceress, especially with the one finger gone. Extreme old age only intensified this effect. She was a tiny bird of a woman now, holding onto the frail ends of life in her Fabergé egg of a house. She was small and shriveled in her long nightgown, and her waist-length hair had gone completely white. She looked, for all the world, like the witch she was meant to be.The wind, it seemed, was ever at his back. Start with the fact of his extraordinary size, at birth more boulder than baby, in his prime more tree than man. His mother delivered him—ten pounds and then some—at home, before the days of anesthesia or caesareans. That he and she survived his birth must be counted as his first stoke of luck. By fifteen he had reached a thriving six-foot-eight and was forever hitting his head on the doorjambs of the old family home in Southampton, New York.As far as John Herrick could tell, those bumps to the noggin were one of the few downsides to being so tall. Otherwise, height conferred distinct advantages. Due to some quirk of primate psychology, people tended to assume, eight times out of ten, that a tall fellow was more capable than the next man, more likely to be a natural leader. That was true of his peers, who admired John for his athleticism and good looks, but the same principle seemed to apply to his dealings with adults, principally those he met in his father's hardware store, where he worked in the summers, ringing up purchases and stocking shelves and showing neighbors the way to switch plates and five-penny nails. Most everyone was happy to talk to this tall young man with the knack for chatting, amiably but honestly, with strangers and his quick way with a joke. Encounters with the “rude rich” (thick upon the ground in Southampton even then) could rankle. But occasional unpleasantness was a small price to pay for a job that taught discipline, and left your afternoons free for golf, or for basketball, or for messing about in the houseboat you'd built with your own hands. It was good to grow up in a town with streets named after your own forebears, with pastures and beaches and byways you were free to explore, almost without restriction. Perhaps there were some near misses among his early adventures, an encounter with thin ice, or a riptide. Somehow or other he always returned to the white house on Main Street, with its highboys and lowboys, Delftware and pewter, and women who knew where every last cruet came from.All this would have been inheritance enough, but there were grander things in store. records.title: Wīnak in Soonkahni: GuateMayans in the Salt Lake Valley
records.abstract: My story is one of being a part of many worlds, and my approach in this essay is based in a global Indigenous perspective. What this means to me is that I have my unique Indigenous experience and worldview that I will share in this essay, while I also seek to uphold respect for different and especially local Indigenous peoples. A global Indigenous perspective includes acknowledging the ways peoples have moved, such as through displacement or migration. This essay emerges out of the question of what it means to reimagine an Indigenous identity and culture after global movement. What happens when you are no longer in an ancestral homeland? There are important differences to keep in mind between the contexts of the “Global North” and the “Global South,” as well as distinctions between how identity is expressed based in ancestry versus living cultural practices. Many present-day Indigenous identities and experiences have also become entwined in modern and Christian religious practices. What does this all become and mean in the geographical-cultural context of Utah?In this article, I use the terms Wīnak and GuateMayan to refer to peoples from Guatemala, words that are more specific than regional identifiers like Latina/o/x. Wīnak (English spelling) or Winaq (Spanish spelling) is the word for “people/person” in many of the Mayan languages still spoken in Iximulew, the Indigenous Maya term for Guatemala.1 The term Wīnak highlights a unique identity marker for people who are usually overlooked and erased under the larger categories of Latina/o/x, Latin American, or Hispana/o/ic. Wīnak also transcends the identity Guatemalteca/o or the slang term Chapín, both of which refer to a general Guatemalan cultural identity. Of course, there are interconnected and intertwined identities and experiences with national, linguistic, and geo-regional categories of Guatemala, the Spanish language, and Latin America. Another term—GuateMaya—has been increasingly used by artists and intellectuals; it challenges a Guatemalan national identity that has historically used some elements of Mayan culture while at the same time marginalizing a Mayan majority population. GuateMaya as a term also speaks to both the Mayan presence in Guatemalan nationalism as well as the Guatemalan national entanglement with Mayan communities. Yet GuateMaya as a term can also be limiting in a Guatemalan context. Iximulew has an Indigenous majority population that comes predominantly from a diverse range of Mayan peoples and languages, but there are also Xinca, Garifuna, and others who are from this shared place. Throughout this essay I use Iximulew and Guatemala, as well as Wīnak/Winaq and GuateMayan, interchangeably. They are not identical equivalents of each other, but for the sake of convenience I use them in that way.There are many locally specific kinds of Winaq found across different ethnolinguistic groups throughout Iximulew, as well as provincial and global fusions found in urban centers. There are also a growing number of Wīnak experiences and peoples found throughout North America and in Soonkahni (Salt Lake Valley in the Shoshone and Goshute language of Newe Dai gwa/Newe Taikwa). Soonkahni is an Indigenous name for the region I grew up in and where I have lived most of my life.2 Soonkahni means “many houses” in Newe Taikwa. The Nuuch (Ute) elder Forrest Cuch refers to this region as one with a legacy of being a buffer zone between Indigenous peoples.3 Today, the state of Utah occupies the territory of eight sovereign Indigenous nations, whose ancestors shared and contested this place long before the contemporary context. Because many Indigenous peoples of this region trace ancestral ties to this land, and contemporarily peoples from around the world now also call this place home, the meaning of “many houses” for Soonkahni is a fitting description for what is currently also known as the Salt Lake Valley.4 This essay, “Wīnak in Soonkahni,” also expressed as “GuateMayans in the Salt Lake Valley,” is only an introduction to a complex group identity and experience that has many layers of relationships in, of, and to this place. This story is filtered through my perspective. My experiences share much in common with others, but they are also unique among the broader community and even in my own family.This article is based in autoethnographic research and storytelling or, as Indigenous studies frameworks assert, story work. Here I share only a bit of the Wīnak story, offering a selection of insights on the movement and distinctiveness of one family group among the global Indigenous peoples found in Soonkahni.My story has many beginnings, but I will begin with my parents. Rodolfo Hernández Tecún and Gladys Zamora Árcia come from both urban and rural experiences in Iximulew. They left Guatemala during a tumultuous moment in the midst of a civil war that lasted thirty-six years. One catalyst of the war was a coup d’état of Guatemala's democratically elected president in 1954, a coup that was sponsored by the United States Central Intelligence Agency.5 State violence throughout this time, including war crimes such as torture and genocide, escalated in the early 1980s, when much of my family left Guatemala and arrived in the United States. My parents found refuge and opportunity through marriage in a temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Tongva territory (Los Angeles, California), where I would later be born. Shortly after giving birth to me, their first child, they moved with their larger extended family clan to the Rose Park neighborhood in the Neme/Newe (Shoshone and Goshute) territories of Soonkahni.6 They came in search of a family-friendly place to raise their children. We were categorized as racialized migrants and often labelled as Mexicans, Latinos, or Hispanics. The complex ancestries and Indigenous roots we carried as Winaq were constantly erased in the social context of Utah. What then does it mean to be Wīnak—Mayan arrivals or descendants living in North America—yet categorized as Latina/o/x? I come from a long line of highland Maya peoples, including K'iche’, Tz'utujil, Mam, and Kaqchikel.7 However, growing up in the US context, where Indigeneity is legally premised on “blood quantum” and tribal enrollment, I learned that I was a different kind of Native. I was not seen as Black either, even though I have some African ancestry, and due to my darker skin, I was never assumed to be European, despite also having that ancestry.I did not really see myself as Hispanic or Latino, even though I was often captured within these categories. I struggled with those labels because they relate to countries that speak Spanish or Latinate languages, and we do not call Native Americans Anglo or Franco in the United States or Canada because they speak English or French as a result of colonization. In Guatemala, the term “ladino” has historically been used to refer to non-Indigenous inhabitants, distinguishing “Indians” from the modern nation's cultural citizenry. “Mestizo,” which generally refers to mixed-race people, is an equivalent term known in the United States. In fact, “ladino” was a word of conflict for me, because of its political meaning in Guatemala, yet I also have ladino identities that I inherit and am related to, which I suggest are also entangled with a Wīnak or GuateMayan identity.8 In the United States, local Indigenous identity is dominated by more of a legal affair of race that deals with a minority people, which does not necessarily require language or cultural knowledge.9 Ladino in the Guatemalan context, on the other hand, often is assumed to refer to mixed American Indian and European people who deny or ignore ethnic ties to an Indigenous ancestry and who have assimilated into a dominant Eurocentric culture. As a Mayan among the scattered diaspora populations across the United States, I was caught between people who were on one hand in this setting having to prove they had Indigenous ancestry legally and racially, and on the other hand, people from Guatemala who undeniably did, yet some of whom were trying to prove they were not Indigenous anymore. I have observed and experienced a wide range of Mayan and ladino identities and expressions in my large family and extended relations locally and internationally. I and much of my family have mixed ancestry—West and North African, Arab, Jewish, Iberian, and Northern European lineages—which to me adds to our Wīnak heritage. However, the primary cultural identity I work through in this essay is grounded in a Guatemalan-Mayan sense of being, due to its prominence in my life. GuateMayan-ness is related to but also distinct from other Mayan groups who are part of modern nations like Mexico, Belize, and Honduras.My parents’ story and that of their children and family clan is one that crosses the global and local crossroads of race, class, gender, religion, and Indigeneity from Iximulew to Turtle Island (North America).10 We have negotiated and reimagined these multiple identities in many contexts simultaneously since our arrival in Soonkahni. The following vignettes offer a glimpse into the experiences of a unique group of Wīnak/GuateMayans who live in Utah.In many highland Mayan communities of Iximulew there is a practice called cuchubal, which means to “collectively contribute” or “we all give.” My father explained to me that cuchubal is when everyone pitches in to a shared pot and each month those who contribute have a turn to take the large amount. This is like a social savings account where you simultaneously invest in the community of participants, often building on kinship groups, and you also have access to a larger amount of material resource once in the year. My father has shared stories with me of significant moments when cuchubal was used and received to benefit a family member. On one occasion, it was the turn of one of the matriarchs in the family to receive the large amount, yet she used it to help out another relative in need. While I learned about cuchubal from Winaq stories of Iximulew, I later realized that my family clan in Utah had adapted this practice to local customs.Christmas is a different affair in Guatemala than it is in Utah, and one of the cultural changes my parents’ generation faced was the commercial and consumer pressures associated with the holiday in Utah. The religious community we are part of also used this holiday as an annual moment where doing service to others included providing Christmas celebration materials (such as toys or food) so those without the means, or newcomers, could participate in the local version of this holiday. I try to imagine the pressure my parents’ generation may have felt from raising children in this context, with its combination of the cultural forces of assimilation and the heavy value US society places on mass consumption. I imagine these factors and more all contributed to their efforts to emulate the stereotypical “white Christmas.” Yet, while I do remember having a US-influenced Christmas at times during my childhood in Utah, it was not until I was a young adult that I learned of the collaboration in our family clan to provide that. The kinship group I refer to includes a unilineal connection of both my matrilineal and patrilineal family, who many times, instead of giving gifts directly to each other's children, would give resources or gifts to the children's parents. The immediate parent or parents were then able to make their own versions of Christmas in their increasingly nuclear family–focused homes. This act supported parents saving face in Utah and among their religious congregations and neighbors.My parents’ generation could also adopt the Santa mythology if they desired, which allowed them to briefly perform US middle-class cultural experiences.
